articles.title: CYP-mediated drug metabolism from fetal life to adulthood.
articles.abstract: Cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes metabolize ~80% of medications administered across the lifespan. Although CYP enzymes have been allocated to different ontogenic classes according to the developmental pattern of their hepatic protein expression, the roles of hormones, which coordinate developmental events and regulate nuclear receptors that control CYP gene expression, remain poorly understood. In addition, as most CYP enzymes have low expression and activity in the fetal liver, fetal CYP-mediated drug metabolism is largely dependent on CYP activity in the maternal liver and placenta. However, CYP activity changes across gestation in an isoform-specific manner, and it has been proposed that concentrations of pregnancy-related hormones (PRH) may be responsible for these changes. Moreover, there is a limited understanding of whether the maternal liver, placenta, and fetal liver respond differently to PRH, thus changing CYP activity during pregnancy in a tissue-specific manner. This review will describe the developmental changes in CYP enzyme expression and activity in the liver and the different regulatory mechanisms contributing to these changes. The current knowledge regarding changes in CYP enzyme expression and activity during pregnancy across the maternal-placental-fetal compartments, and the impact of PRH on the expression and activity of CYP enzymes, will be discussed.

articles.title: Nanoengineering strategies for precision regulation of chimeric antigen receptor T-cell-induced cytokine release syndrome.
articles.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy faces a critical clinical hurdle: cytokine release syndrome (CRS). Current CRS management strategies have limited selectivity and may interfere with CAR-T cell antitumor activity, highlighting the need for more targeted and precisely controllable interventions. Nanoengineering offers a promising approach to address these limitations by enabling the spatiotemporally controlled monitoring and modulation of inflammatory responses, with the potential to mitigate excessive cytokine release while preserving CAR-T cell therapeutic efficacy, driving a paradigm shift toward programmable, proactive immune regulation. This review systematically examines nanointervention strategies for mitigating CAR-T-induced CRS, including molecular monitoring, cytokine clearance, targeted delivery, stimulus-responsive systems, biomimetic designs, and genetic reprogramming. These approaches enable precise intervention across multiple stages-from early inflammation detection and localized neutralization to source-level cellular engineering. Finally, we discuss challenges in biosafety, clinical translation, and the potential of artificial intelligence-driven predictive platforms. Nanotechnology offers a transformative pathway to redefine CRS from an unpredictable complication into a manageable therapeutic window, paving the way for safer next-generation cellular immunotherapies.

articles.title: Macrophage-centered resistance programs in cancer: A unified framework for therapeutic resistance and precision immunotherapy.
articles.abstract: Therapeutic resistance remains a major barrier to durable cancer control despite advances in immunotherapy, targeted therapy, cellular therapies, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy. Although tumor cell-intrinsic genetic and epigenetic alterations are well-established drivers of resistance, treatment outcomes are also shaped by dynamic interactions within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Among its stromal and immune constituents, tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are prominent regulators of therapeutic resistance because of their functional plasticity and capacity to integrate diverse environmental signals. Here, we introduce macrophage-centered resistance programs as an integrative framework comprising four recurrent, non-mutually exclusive functional modules: lipid-associated, matrix-remodeling, glyco-immune, and metabolic programs. These modules link tumor-derived stressors to macrophage adaptation, immune suppression, stromal remodeling, and therapeutic persistence, while allowing substantial overlap, context dependence, and dynamic interconversion. We further distinguish associative observations from mechanistic and causal evidence and examine how macrophage-associated resistance mechanisms interact with treatment-specific tumor cell-intrinsic pathways across immune checkpoint blockade, cellular therapy, targeted therapy, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy. Finally, we discuss macrophage-directed therapeutic strategies and the requirements for biomarker-guided precision immunotherapy, including clinical validation, assay standardization, and longitudinal monitoring. This framework is intended as a testable organizational model for understanding macrophage-mediated therapeutic resistance and guiding more precise macrophage-directed interventions.

articles.title: α-tocopherol (Vitamin E) inhibits second mitochondria-derived activator of caspases (SMAC) mimetic-induced cell death by directly targeting cIAP1 degradation.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Tocopherols (vitamin E) are well characterized as essential lipophilic antioxidant agents. However, recent evidence suggests that tocopherols may also regulate cellular signalling through direct interactions with specific protein targets. This study aimed to investigate the molecular mechanism by which α-tocopherol regulates programmed cell death and to identify its direct molecular target. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: A high-throughput screen identified α-tocopherol as an inhibitor of TNF-α/SMAC-mimetic-induced cell death. The mechanism(s) underlying this action of α-tocopherol was investigated using western blotting, immunoprecipitation, ubiquitination assays, drug affinity responsive target stability, cellular thermal shift assay, isothermal titration calorimetry and molecular docking. Its efficacy, in vivo, was evaluated in a murine model of ulcerative colitis, induced by dextran sulphate sodium (DSS). KEY RESULTS: α-Tocopherol selectively inhibited TNF-α/SMAC-mimetic-induced cell death by directly and competitively binding to the BIR3 domain of the inhibitor of apoptosis protein-1 (cIAP1). This interaction stabilized cIAP1, prevented the formation of RIPK1-dependent death complexes and suppressed apoptosis and necroptosis. In a murine model of DSS-induced colitis, α-tocopherol significantly alleviated disease severity while preserving cIAP1 protein expression. CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: Our findings identified cIAP1 as a previously unrecognized molecular target of α-tocopherol and demonstrated that cIAP1 stabilization contributed to the suppression of RIPK1-dependent cell death. These findings expand the current understanding of the biological functions of tocopherols and provide a mechanistic basis for their potential therapeutic application in inflammatory diseases associated with aberrant cIAP1 degradation.

articles.title: Mangiferin Buffers Depressive-Like Behaviors by Modulating Astrocytic DHHC2 in the Hippocampus.
articles.abstract: Several lines of evidence indicate that mangiferin (MGF) ameliorates chronic stress-induced anxiety- and depressive-like behaviors, yet its precise role and underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we show that MGF effectively alleviates anxiety- and depressive-like behaviors in mice exposed to chronic stress, accompanied by reduced synaptic loss and ameliorated hippocampal neurogenesis deficits. Notably, nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) expression is preferentially altered in hippocampal astrocytes but not in neurons or microglia after chronic stress and MGF treatment, and knockdown of astrocytic Nrf2 abrogates the antidepressant effect of MGF. Further mechanistic studies showed that MGF reverses reactive astrogliosis by regulating astrocytic DHHC2-Nrf2 signaling, including Nrf2 palmitoylation and its nuclear translocation, thereby protecting Nrf2 from Keap1-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation and sustaining its transcriptional activity in reactive astrocytes. These findings demonstrate that MGF alleviates chronic stress-induced anxiety- and depressive-like behaviors by engaging the astrocytic DHHC2-Nrf2 signaling, suppressing reactive astrogliosis and reversing hippocampal synaptic and neurogenic deficits, which provides novel insights into the therapeutic potential of MGF for chronic stress-related mood disorders.

articles.title: Temporal and Spatial Dynamics and Mechanisms of Brain-Gut Axis Injury Induced by Confinement-Like Physical Restraint Stress in Mice.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Long-term SIS exposure across aerospace, deep-sea, underground, and quarantine settings increases depression and gut-brain axis dysfunction risk, but long-term nonlinear injury dynamics remain poorly understood. METHODS: We analyzed GBD 2023 depression burden data in adults aged 15-49, then established a 0-35 day (d) chronic restraint stress mouse model that isolates the core physical confinement and activity-restriction component of SIS. Integrating behavior, histology, biochemistry, 16S sequencing, metabolomics, and formal nonlinear changepoint analysis, we validated picolinic acid (PLA) effects via in vivo intervention, in silico docking, and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT). RESULTS: Population data showed that the global depression burden during the COVID-19 period followed a rapid rise-partial recovery-persistent disability pattern, providing a temporal reference for the experimental model. In mice, confinement-like restraint stress induced triphasic nonlinear gut-brain injury with changepoints at ~7 and ~21 days: early HPA/inflammatory activation, mid-phase gut barrier disruption and anxiety-like behavior, and late hippocampal damage with despair-like behavior. Microbiota remodeling and tryptophan metabolic shift formed the core signaling cascade, with PLA identified as the key gut-brain metabolite. Exogenous PLA dose-dependently improved depressive phenotypes, repaired barriers, and suppressed HPA hyperactivity and inflammation. FMT provided suggestive evidence that gut microbiota contribute to PLA's protective effects. CONCLUSION: Chronic confinement-like restraint stress induces triphasic nonlinear gut-brain axis injury rather than linear damage. PLA is a promising candidate target for mental health protection in isolated, confined, extreme environment populations and stress-related depression intervention.

articles.title: An anti-ferroptosis hydrogel enhances mesenchymal stem cell spheroid-based gene delivery for spinal cord injury repair.
articles.abstract: Stem cell-based gene delivery systems represent a promising approach for sustained and localized therapeutic factor delivery after spinal cord injury (SCI). However, their in vivo performance is often limited by poor graft survival in the hostile lesion microenvironment. Here, using glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) as a representative therapeutic cargo, we established a mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) spheroid (MS)-based GDNF gene delivery system (GF-MS). Notably, we identified that ferroptosis served as an important and targetable limiting factor restricting graft persistence and transgene output in SCI rats, as supported by transcriptomic enrichment of ferroptosis-related pathways, mitochondrial damage, ferrous iron accumulation, excessive lipid peroxidation, impaired SLC7A11/GPX4 antioxidant defense, and reduced GDNF expression in implanted GF-MS. To overcome this limitation, we constructed a ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1)-loaded reactive oxygen species (ROS)-scavenging hydrogel (RH-Fer), which can scavenge excessive microenvironmental ROS and responsively release Fer-1. In vivo experiments demonstrated that RH-Fer effectively mitigated ferroptosis and prolonged graft persistence of GF-MS. Consequently, this combined system enhanced local GDNF expression during the therapeutic window and promoted neural tissue repair and functional recovery in SCI rats. These findings highlight ferroptosis-targeted microenvironment modulation as an effective strategy to optimize stem cell-based gene delivery for SCI repair.

articles.title: Machine learning-guided multimodal analysis of APAF1-associated tumor microenvironment features prioritizes morellic acid for gastric cancer.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Gastric cancer (GC) exhibits substantial molecular heterogeneity and a complex tumor microenvironment (TME). Apoptotic protease-activating factor 1 (APAF1) is a core component of mitochondrial apoptosis; however, its association with immune characteristics, spatial heterogeneity and compound discovery in GC remains poorly defined. METHODS: The bulk transcriptomics, single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics with machine learning-based modeling, immune deconvolution and spatial niche analysis were integrated to characterize APAF1-associated features in GC. Machine learning-guided computational screening combining molecular docking and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations was used to prioritize morellic acid (MA). The biological effects of MA and the involvement of APAF1-associated signaling were evaluated through in vitro and in vivo assays using APAF1-targeting siRNA and shRNA, respectively. RESULTS: APAF1 expression was increased in GC, particularly in early-stage tumors and was independently associated with improved overall survival after multivariable adjustment (HR = 0.681, 95% CI: 0.494-0.940, P = 0.0196). However, its standalone prognostic discrimination was limited, with time-dependent ROC analyses showing poor predictive performance. Tumor-versus-normal ROC analysis demonstrated differential expression between GC and normal tissues (AUC = 0.875, 95% CI: 0.823-0.918). Single-cell and spatial analyses revealed that APAF1 expression was associated with distinct immune-cell patterns and tumor spatial niches. Machine learning-guided computational screening prioritized MA as a candidate compound. MA inhibited GC cell proliferation and migration (IC50: 1.807 ± 0.16 to 6.216 ± 0.23 μM) and suppressed tumor growth in vivo, achieving tumor inhibition rates of 79.32 ± 7.69%, 92.37 ± 4.21%, and 92.19 ± 2.99% at low, medium and high doses, respectively. APAF1 silencing attenuated MA-associated changes in cleaved Caspase-3 activation and GSDME-NT accumulation, suggesting the involvement of APAF1-associated cell-death signaling. CONCLUSION: APAF1 is associated with distinct tumor microenvironment characteristics and clinical features in GC, supporting its potential relevance to tumor biology beyond its canonical role in mitochondrial apoptosis. The novelty of this study lies in extending the investigation of APAF1 beyond its canonical apoptotic function by integrating machine learning with multimodal transcriptomic and spatial analyses to characterize APAF1-associated TME features and computationally prioritize MA. All the findings provide a cross-scale framework linking APAF1-associated tumor biology with candidate compound screening and MA-related cell-death responses in GC.

articles.title: Single-cell and spatial analysis of inflammation-associated resistance in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma.
articles.abstract: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC) is frequently associated with chronic inflammation and a complex stromal microenvironment, yet the cellular and molecular features underlying heterogeneous responses to neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy remain unclear. Here, using Flex-based single-cell transcriptomic profiling of post-treatment ICC specimens from responders and non-responders, together with multiplex immunohistochemistry and animal model validation, we delineate a coordinated, inflammation-associated multicellular state linked to treatment non-response. Non-response tumors showed enrichment of SPINK1⁺ epithelial cells, inflammatory cancer-associated fibroblasts, SPP1⁺ and inflammatory macrophage states, and immunosuppressive or inflammation-associated CD4⁺ T-cell programs. Across epithelial, stromal, and immune compartments, IL6-JAK-STAT3-related inflammatory signaling emerged as a recurrent feature of resistance. Computational cell-cell communication analysis predicted increased communication probabilities between iCAFs and SPINK1⁺ epithelial cells and between InfMp and CD4Tem cells in non-response tumors, nominating TNF-TLR2, HMGB1-TLR2, AGT-CYBB, and TNF-ICAM1 as candidate ligand-receptor associations. Tissue-level validation confirmed increased SPINK1 expression, inflammatory macrophage features, and elevated p-STAT3 signals in non-response tumors. Combined PD-1 blockade and JAK1/2 inhibition showed enhanced antitumor activity in both a hydrodynamic injection-based cholangiocarcinoma-like mouse model and a humanized huPBMC-NOG-dKO mouse model bearing ICC-X1 xenografts. In the hydrodynamic model, the combination was also accompanied by reduced p-STAT3 activity and enhanced T-cell infiltration and granzyme B expression. Together, these findings identify a coordinated, multicellular inflammatory state associated with non-response to neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy in ICC and nominate JAK-STAT signaling as a convergent, therapeutically actionable vulnerability. The antitumor activity observed with combined JAK1/2 inhibition and PD-1 blockade further supports evaluating this inflammatory signaling axis as a therapeutic target to improve immunotherapy responsiveness in ICC.

articles.title: Qiliqiangxin Capsule ameliorates post-myocardial infarction heart failure: associations with gut microbiota remodeling, altered fecal short-chain fatty acid profiles, and myocardial HDAC3-associated histone acetylation and JNK/TGF-β-related signaling.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Qiliqiangxin Capsule (QLQX) is a guideline-recommended adjunctive therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, but mechanisms underlying post-myocardial infarction heart failure (post-MI HF) remain incompletely defined, particularly gut-heart microbial metabolism. PURPOSE: This study aimed to characterize the gut microbial and fecal short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) alterations associated with the cardioprotective effects of QLQX and to determine whether gut-associated factors contribute functionally to its therapeutic effects in post-MI HF. METHODS: A rat model of post-MI HF was established by permanent ligation of the left anterior descending coronary artery. Cardiac function, ventricular remodeling, histopathological injury, and inflammatory indices were evaluated after QLQX treatment. An integrated analytical strategy comprising fecal 16S rRNA gene sequencing, targeted fecal SCFA quantification, untargeted fecal and myocardial metabolomics, myocardial transcriptomics, and targeted protein analyses was used to characterize gut and cardiac responses. A publicly available human ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction transcriptomic dataset was included for exploratory pathway-level comparison. Spearman correlation analysis with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction was performed to examine associations among microbial taxa, SCFAs, inflammatory markers, and cardiac functional indices. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations were used to assess the structural plausibility of selected candidate interactions, and surface plasmon resonance (SPR) was performed to experimentally evaluate the predicted interaction between isobutyrate and JNK1. Antibiotic treatment and fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) were further performed to evaluate the functional contribution and transferability of gut-associated fecal factors. RESULTS: QLQX improved cardiac dysfunction, adverse ventricular remodeling, myocardial injury, and inflammatory responses in post-MI HF rats. Treatment reshaped the fecal microbial community and altered the fecal SCFA profile, including restoration of butyrate and isobutyrate. Selected SCFAs and bacterial taxa were associated with inflammatory markers and cardiac functional indices. Integrated omics and protein analyses further showed that these gut-associated alterations were accompanied by coordinated changes in myocardial cAMP, nuclear HDAC3 abundance, histone H3 acetylation, AMPK/mTOR signaling, and JNK/TGF-β related molecular indices. SPR analysis further demonstrated concentration-dependent binding of isobutyrate to JNK1, with an equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) of 5.89 × 10⁻⁵ M. Antibiotic treatment attenuated the therapeutic response to QLQX, whereas FMT from QLQX-treated donors partially transferred the protective phenotype, supporting a functional contribution of fecally transferable gut-associated factors. CONCLUSION: QLQX ameliorated post-MI HF in association with remodeling of the gut microbial ecosystem, alterations in fecal SCFA profiles, and coordinated myocardial metabolic, epigenetic, and stress-signaling responses. The antibiotic and FMT experiments suggest that gut-associated factors partly contribute to the cardioprotective effects of QLQX. Butyrate and isobutyrate emerged as prioritized candidate metabolites, with SPR providing direct binding evidence for the isobutyrate-JNK1 interaction, although their broader causal roles and myocardial exposure require further validation.

articles.title: Siwei Dihuang Pill ameliorates postmenopausal osteosarcopenia: Multi-omics insights into arachidonic acid metabolism and PTGER4/CREB/SIRT1-related signaling in gut-bone-muscle crosstalk.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Siwei Dihuang Pill (SWDHP), a traditional Chinese herbal formula, has shown beneficial effects on estrogen deficiency-associated osteosarcopenia (OS), but its systemic mechanisms remain unclear. OBJECTIVE: To investigate the effects of SWDHP on postmenopausal OS and the associated mechanisms from the perspective of gut-bone-muscle crosstalk. METHODS: An ovariectomized rat model was used to evaluate SWDHP efficacy. Serum-absorbed compounds were characterized by UHPLC-Q-Orbitrap HRMS. Integrated multi-omics analyses were combined with targeted LC-MS/MS quantification of fecal arachidonic acid (AA) and PGE2, cAMP measurement, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, SPR, RT-qPCR, and Western blotting. RESULTS: SWDHP alleviated bone loss, skeletal muscle atrophy, and colonic inflammation. Multi-omics analyses revealed coordinated changes in gut microbiota, Th17/Treg-associated immune markers, oxidative stress-related indices, and osteoclast differentiation, and highlighted AA metabolism as a pathway associated with OS-related multisystem dysfunction. SWDHP increased PTGER4 expression and cAMP levels, accompanied by enhanced PKA/CREB phosphorylation, increased SIRT1 expression, and reduced NF-κB signaling. Kaempferol showed favorable predicted interactions with PTGER4 and SIRT1, while SPR demonstrated direct binding to SIRT1 (KD = 15.73 μM). CONCLUSION: SWDHP alleviates postmenopausal OS, accompanied by coordinated alterations in gut microbiota, AA metabolism, and PTGER4/CREB/SIRT1-related signaling across the gut-bone-muscle axis.

articles.title: Mechanistic Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Extended-Release Metformin in Obese South African Women Living with HIV on Dolutegravir.
articles.abstract: Regulatory limits on metformin co-administered with dolutegravir (DTG) derive from healthy-volunteer studies in which DTG increased metformin exposure by 79% through organic cation transporter 2 inhibition, prompting a 1,000 mg/day metformin dose restriction. Whether this applies to women with HIV and severe obesity, a clinically important and understudied population for metformin-DTG coadministration, is unknown. In a secondary analysis of a reported cohort, we developed a population pharmacokinetic model of extended-release (XR) metformin with a zero-order-release, first-order-absorption structure scaled by lean body mass (LBM). Estimated glomerular filtration rate and DTG exposure were evaluated as clearance covariates, including DTG as a time-varying competitive inhibitor. We simulated steady-state exposures across body mass index (BMI) 30-60 kg/m2 at 1000-3000 mg once daily compared to a DTG-free reference model. Fifteen women contributed evaluable profiles (mean BMI 45.6 kg/m2). Apparent clearance was 70.2 L/h, approximately 40% higher than reported non-obese values, and DTG exposure was approximately 54% lower than in volunteer studies. LBM dominated clearance and volume, while no DTG exposure-dependent effect on metformin clearance was identifiable within the observed low DTG exposure range. Simulated exposures rose near-proportionally with dose and minimally with BMI; the proportion exceeding the lactic acidosis-associated maximum concentration of 5 mg/L was 4.4% at 2000 mg/day, 16.9% at 2500 mg/day and 37.9% at 3000 mg/day, whereas none exceeded the lactic acidosis-associated average steady-state concentration of 4 mg/L. Although an interaction at higher DTG exposures cannot be excluded, the low exposures observed suggest the 1,000 mg/day restriction may underdose this obese population, supporting investigation of doses up to 2000 mg/day as the maximum authorized daily dose for metformin XR.

articles.title: Implementation of Pharmacogenomics in Pediatric-Focused Institutions Within the Pharmacogenomics Global Research Network.
articles.abstract: Descriptions of how pediatric-focused institutions implement pharmacogenomic testing are scarce, and often not differentiated from adult-focused institutions. We aimed to provide a detailed description of how pediatric-focused institutions across the world implemented pharmacogenomic testing in clinical practice. A survey was distributed to members of the Pharmacogenomics Global Research Network to assess program infrastructure, implementation efforts, genes tested, method of testing, and clinical decision support. The survey was completed by 43 institutions that have implemented pharmacogenomics: 12 pediatric-focused, 10 adult-focused, and 21 institutions serving all ages. All pediatric-focused institutions provide testing for CYP2C19, CYP2C9, CYP2D6, CYP3A5, NUDT15, and TPMT. Psychiatry and hematology/oncology were the specialties most commonly reported as implementing pharmacogenomics at pediatric-focused institutions. Most institutions have clinical decision support incorporated into their electronic health record and a similar number of compensated employees contributing to the program, regardless of age group focus. All pediatric-focused institutions were non-profit and often received programmatic funding from internal sources. A higher proportion of pediatric-focused sites provided patient education (92%) compared to adult-focused (60%) and those caring for all ages (76%). Pediatric-focused institutions interested in implementing or expanding their pharmacogenomic services will encounter many of the same opportunities and considerations as adult institutions. The results of this survey highlight additional unique considerations for pediatric-focused pharmacogenomic implementation and may serve as a roadmap for pediatric institutions interested in implementing or expanding pharmacogenomic services.

articles.title: Efficacy and safety of commercial Chinese polyherbal preparations combined with biomedicine for elderly patients with primary insomnia: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The prevalence of primary insomnia among the elderly is steadily increasing; however, robust evidence supporting the efficacy and safety of combining commercial Chinese polyherbal preparations (CCPPs) with biomedicine therapy remains insufficient. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of CCPPs combined with biomedicine versus biomedicine therapy for primary insomnia in elderly patients, and to assess the certainty of the evidence via the GRADE framework and P-curve analysis. METHODS: Seven biomedical databases were searched (before November 2025) for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving elderly patients with primary insomnia. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane RoB 2 by two researchers independently. Meta-analysis was performed using R software. Outcomes included Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), total clinical effectiveness rate, Sleep Dysfunction Rating Scale (SDRS), and adverse events. Robustness was evaluated via sensitivity, subgroup, and P-curve analyses. RESULTS: Meta-analysis suggested that combined therapy was associated with a lower PSQI score (MD = -2.09, 95% CI -2.62 to -1.57) and higher total clinical effectiveness rate (RR = 1.21, 95% CI 1.15-1.27) relative to monotherapy. The combination group also showed a lower risk of adverse events (RR = 0.47, 95% CI 0.36-0.61). However, P-curve analysis revealed notable discrepancies across outcomes: PSQI exhibited sufficient evidential value (Power = 99%), whereas the total clinical effectiveness rate lacked adequate evidential value (Power = 9%), implying potential publication bias. Subgroup analyses showed that heterogeneity decreased within the subgroup of patients with disease duration <1 year, although the between-subgroup difference did not reach statistical significance. The certainty of evidence was rated as "Moderate" for adverse events but "Low" to "Very Low" for efficacy outcomes. CONCLUSION: In elderly patients with primary insomnia, combined treatment of CCPPs and biomedicine may help improve sleep quality and may reduce adverse events reported in clinical trials. However, due to methodological limitations, high heterogeneity and potential publication bias among the included trials, the certainty of the available evidence remains limited. Given insufficient evidential value, the reliability of the total clinical effectiveness rate is questionable, and clinicians should place greater emphasis on outcomes assessed using validated scales such as the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Further large-scale, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are needed to further verify these preliminary findings. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251186213, identifier: CRD420251186213.

articles.title: A novel MST1-targeting kinsenoside derivative K30 attenuates acute kidney injury by restoring mitochondrial homeostasis.
articles.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a heterogeneous syndrome with limited treatments, underscoring the need for new therapies. The natural glycoside kinsenoside is a promising candidate owing to its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. We synthesized a series of kinsenoside derivatives and identified K30 as the most effective nephroprotective compound. In murine models of cisplatin-, folic acid-, and ischemia-reperfusion-induced AKI, K30 significantly preserved renal function, attenuated inflammation and oxidative stress, ameliorated mitochondrial dysfunction, and showed no evident systemic toxicity. Cellular thermal shift assay combined with mass spectrometry identified mammalian STE20-like kinase 1 (MST1) as the direct target of K30, which was further validated by drug affinity responsive target stability assays, molecular docking, surface plasmon resonance, and in vitro kinase activity assays. The renoprotective effect of K30 was abolished in MST1-knockdown cells and restored upon MST1 re-expression, and its efficacy was comparable to two established MST1 inhibitors. Mechanistically, K30 exerts its renoprotective effect by directly targeting and inhibiting MST1, thus suppressing the downstream JNK-Drp1 signaling axis, which in turn ameliorates pathological mitochondrial fission. These results demonstrate that K30 is an effective MST1-targeting compound capable of maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis, highlighting its potential as a novel therapeutic agent for AKI.

articles.title: Regulatory lessons from FDA review of approved AAV gene therapies.
Decision quality in biopharma portfolio renewal.
Gut-active polysaccharide carriers for colonic 5-ASA delivery in ulcerative colitis.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Ulcerative colitis (UC) affects approximately 4.9 million people worldwide, with incidence rising globally and prevalence approaching 1% in industrialized nations. 5-Aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) is first-line therapy for mild-to-moderately active UC, yet pooled endoscopic mucosal healing averages only approximately 37% and 10-year relapse approaches 67%. A central reason is ineffective drug delivery: current technologies release 5-ASA into the bulk lumen, and pH-dependent coatings fail in active UC, where intracolonic pH is variable. Mucosal tissue concentration, not luminal concentration, determines efficacy, and concurrent gut dysbiosis sustains inflammation that current 5-ASA formulations fail to address. AREAS COVERED: UC-associated gut dysbiosis, the limitations of current colonic 5-ASA delivery, and gut-active polysaccharide carriers (inulin and modified inulin, pectin, guar gum, konjac glucomannan [KGM], resistant starch, and hyaluronic acid [HA]) applied specifically to 5-ASA. Advanced nanoparticle and hydrogel platforms and translational and regulatory priorities are also discussed. EXPERT OPINION: Gut-active, enzyme-responsive polysaccharide carriers are a rational formulation strategy for UC. By coupling colonic 5-ASA release to microbial fermentation at the mucosal interface, they deliver drug closer to the epithelial target while generating short-chain fatty acids (SCFA) that may attenuate dysbiosis. Since release is enzyme-triggered rather than pH-dependent, these systems can overcome the dissolution failure that limits current 5-ASA delivery.

articles.title: Semi-randomized zwitterionic peptides: a breakthrough in drug delivery.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Nanoparticle drug delivery systems (NP DDS) have transformed therapeutic delivery by improving drug stability, extending circulation time, and enabling targeted biodistribution. However, clinical translation remains limited by protein corona formation, immune recognition, and accelerated blood clearance following repeated administration. Poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) has been the gold-standard antifouling material for decades, but emerging anti-PEG immune responses have driven the search for alternative stealth technologies. AREAS COVERED: Zwitterionic peptides (ZIPs) have emerged as a promising class of antifouling materials because they combine the hydration-mediated stealth properties of zwitterionic polymers with the molecular precision and programmability of peptide synthesis. Here, ZIP applications in drug delivery were reviewed using the Web of Science database from 2014-2026, focusing on reducing and controlling the protein corona, recent advances in ZIP-based drug delivery, and the potential of high-throughput screening platforms and machine learning-guided ZIP design. Recent studies suggest that biological interactions of ZIP-functionalized NPs are governed primarily by charge motifs rather than precise sequences, creating new opportunities for material design. EXPERT OPINION: This observation motivates developing semi-randomized ZIPs (srZIPs) that preserve charge organization while introducing sequence diversity. By maintaining key physicochemical and biological properties while diversifying composition, srZIPs may reduce immune recognition without sacrificing antifouling function.

articles.title: Targeting the metabolism-autophagy-ferroptosis interactome in cancer drug resistance: molecular targets, structural pharmacology, and combination strategies.
articles.abstract: Cancer drug resistance can involve both genetic alterations and reversible changes in metabolism, stress responses, and susceptibility to cell death.Metabolic reprogramming, autophagy, and ferroptosis are closely connected in this process: metabolic adaptation sustains energy and antioxidant production and remodels membrane lipids; autophagy buffers therapeutic stress through nutrient recycling and organelle quality control; and ferroptosis-defense systems limit lethal phospholipid peroxidation. Their interactions can stabilize treatment-tolerant states, although the direction and importance of each process vary by tumor lineage, treatment history, and microenvironment. This review evaluates molecular nodes connecting these processes, with emphasis on GPX4, SLC7A11/xCT, the NCOA4-FTH1 ferritinophagy interface, the USP18-hyperoside (HYP; not to be confused with hypericin) axis, WWP1, ENO1, and DHODH. In this review, we compare interventions using explicit evidence criteria: physical target engagement, causal contribution to a defined resistant phenotype, and pathway association when direct engagement or resistance causality has not been established. We also assess how experimentally determined structures, selective autophagic cargo, parallel ferroptosis-defense systems, tumor context, and translational constraints affect the interpretation of resistance-reversal claims. This framework is intended to distinguish mechanistic plausibility from pharmacologically actionable evidence.

articles.title: Peroxidasin in extracellular matrix remodeling: Structure, catalytic mechanisms, pathological roles, and pharmacological modulation.
articles.abstract: Peroxidasin (PXDN) is a multidomain extracellular heme peroxidase that uses hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) to oxidize bromide (Br-) to hypobromous acid (HOBr), thereby promoting sulfilimine bond formation between adjacent non-collagenous 1 (NC1) domains of collagen IV and maintaining basement membrane integrity. Beyond this canonical reaction, PXDN may regulate extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling through broader oxidative or brominating modifications of extracellular proteins. Dysregulated PXDN expression or activity has been associated with pathological ECM remodeling in fibrosis, cancer, renal disease, vascular disorders, and other matrix-related conditions. This review discusses PXDN domain organization, heme-dependent catalysis, ECM-associated functions, pathological remodeling, and current pharmacological approaches to PXDN modulation. Published pharmacological data are considered alongside predicted ligand interactions within the PXDN heme pocket.

articles.title: The RGS4-Gαq/11 axis in vascular homeostasis: Mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
articles.abstract: Vascular homeostasis, a dynamic equilibrium maintained by the circulatory system, is fundamental to cardiovascular health. Its dysregulation underlies the pathogenesis of major cardiovascular disorders, including hypertension. G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), a versatile family of seven-transmembrane proteins, play a central role in maintaining vascular homeostasis. Upon activation, certain GPCRs couple to Gαq/11 proteins and initiate multiple downstream signaling pathways, thereby regulating vascular tone, structural remodeling, and inflammatory responses. Regulator of G protein signaling 4 (RGS4) functions as a key GTPase-activating protein (GAP) that markedly accelerates GTP hydrolysis by Gαq/11, thereby promoting the timely termination of Gαq/11-mediated signaling. RGS4 therefore plays an important role in maintaining the balance of G protein signaling in the vasculature. Based on the three-dimensional structure of RGS4 (PDB ID: 1AGR), this review systematically delineates the GAP catalytic mechanism of RGS4 and its interactions with downstream effectors, including Gαq/11 and PLCβ. It discusses the pathological role of the RGS4-Gαq/11 signaling axis in major cardiovascular disorders. In addition, from a structural pharmacology perspective, this review surveys the druggable features of RGS4 and reviews previously published in silico docking and molecular dynamics studies of its representative inhibitors, intending to inform potential therapeutic strategies targeting the RGS4-Gαq/11 axis in cardiovascular disease.

articles.title: Stability-indicating reversed-phase liquid chromatography for fixed-dose combination pharmaceutical products: A systematic review and critical appraisal.
articles.abstract: Stability-indicating reversed-phase liquid chromatography is widely used in pharmaceutical quality testing, but the evidential strength of published claims for fixed-dose combination (FDC) products has not been systematically evaluated. This systematic review evaluated primary analytical-method studies published from 2020 through 14 September 2026 using PubMed, OpenAlex, Crossref, Google Scholar, and citation searching. Eligibility required a genuine combined finished product and, as a review-specific scope criterion, at least one qualifying forced-degradation experiment linked to that product or to a directly product-derived preparation. The final dataset comprised 143 studies encompassing 144 independent RP-LC methods (124 assay-only, 13 impurities-only and seven supporting both purposes), 322 analyte-level rows and 1,766 API × stress rows. Following author-approved source-metric adjudication of 94 historical API × stress observations, among 1,673 qualifying API × stress rows, 31.0% were in the <5% band, 28.0% in the 5-20% band, 35.8% were classified as Not assessable, and 5.2% were in the >20% band; these source-heterogeneous classes are not a uniform independently verified measure of API chemical degradation. RP-HPLC was used in 80.4% of studies and PDA/DAD detection in 81.8%. Explicit peak-purity evidence was reported in 53.8%, mass balance in 11.9%, degradant assignment in 17.5%, and orthogonal structural identification in 2.1%; 48.3% contained material reporting inconsistencies. Critical-appraisal ratings were Strong in 23.1%, Moderate in 51.0%, and Limited in 25.9%. Published methods show broad stress coverage but uneven evidential depth, particularly in challenge assessment, degradant support, structural characterization, and reporting integrity.

articles.title: Beyond the brain: curcumin as a multi-target neuropharmacological modulator of the gut-brain axis in major depressive disorder and Parkinson's disease.
articles.abstract: Curcumin, the principal polyphenol of Curcuma longa, has been proposed as a multi-target neuropharmacological agent for neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. We propose that major depressive disorder (MDD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) share a convergent gut-brain axis dysfunction, and that curcumin can serve as a pharmacological probe to test whether this convergent pathway is causally relevant. This narrative review evaluates that hypothesis. We conducted a structured literature search across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and CNKI using predefined search terms. This is a narrative review with a structured search strategy rather than a systematic review; no formal risk-of-bias assessment or meta-analysis was performed. From 2256 identified records, 112 primary studies were selected for synthesis after dual screening and consensus resolution. Findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than as a quantitative synthesis. We propose a differential metabolite-sensitivity threshold model as a testable hypothesis: shared dysbiosis-related metabolic and inflammatory disturbances may affect serotonergic function earlier than dopaminergic function because depressed mood manifests at modest neurotransmitter deficits, whereas nigrostriatal dopaminergic neurons possess substantial compensatory reserve. Preclinical studies indicate that curcumin exerts prebiotic-like effects, promotes short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria, suppresses NF-κB-dependent neuroinflammation, restores BDNF signaling, inhibits α-synuclein aggregation, and improves depressive- and PD-like behaviors. These actions map onto convergent gut-brain pathways involving short-chain fatty acid deficiency, tryptophan-kynurenine imbalance, monoaminergic precursor depletion, and neuroinflammation. This model generates four testable predictions: (P1: functional dysbiosis convergence; P2: temporal precedence of depressed mood; P3: curcumin's multi-node modulation; and P4: clinical benefit with adequate bioavailability). Preclinical evidence supports functional convergence (P1), temporal asymmetry (P2), and curcumin's multi-target actions (P3), but clinical benefit in MDD-PD comorbidity (P4) remains untested. However, curcumin's clinical translation remains limited by poor oral bioavailability (~ 1% for standard extracts) and the absence of randomized trials in MDD-PD comorbidity. We conclude that the convergent gut-brain hypothesis is plausible, partially supported, and directly testable, and we specify the minimal studies required to confirm or falsify it.

articles.title: Safety profiles of current and emerging neoadjuvant immune-modulatory and combination strategies in borderline resectable stage III non-small cell lung cancer: a narrative review.
articles.abstract: Borderline resectable stage III non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) has no consensus definition. In an international multidisciplinary survey of stage III TNM subsets, no agreement on resectability was reached for 11 of 37 subsets, and the multisocietal consensus exercise conducted alongside it left the same anatomical configurations unresolved. This review adopts those non-consensus subsets as its working definition and asks how the safety profiles of current and emerging neoadjuvant immune-modulatory and combination strategies, spanning PD-1 and PD-L1 blockade, emerging checkpoint and immune-metabolic targets, antibody-drug conjugates and bispecific antibodies, bear on surgical decision-making within them. Six phase 3 trials now support neoadjuvant or perioperative PD-1 or PD-L1 blockade with platinum doublet chemotherapy in resectable disease, with pathological complete response rates of 17.2%-40.7% and event-free survival hazard ratios of 0.40-0.68. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse events ranged from 32.5% to 73.0%, immune-mediated adverse events from 25.3% to 42.1% where an aggregate was reported, and treatment-related cancellation of surgery remained below 2% in every trial reporting it. Most patients who never reached resection did so for reasons other than toxicity. Among emerging targets, monospecific TIGIT blockade has failed in three randomised settings and the most advanced TIM-3 programme was discontinued on company-reported evidence, which recontextualises the earlier phase 2 signals for both classes. NKG2A, CD73 and TROP2-directed combinations have produced neoadjuvant pathological response signals without loss of surgical feasibility, although each rests on a single-arm platform cohort of fewer than 80 patients. One PD-1 and VEGF bispecific antibody has positive peer-reviewed phase 3 data in advanced disease and no neoadjuvant data. The operative question in borderline resectable disease is not whether response rates rise but whether toxicity, surgical delay and functional decline shift the risk-benefit balance in patients already marginal for resection. Answering it requires prospective cohorts in which borderline status is defined before treatment, of which MDT-BRIDGE and NEOINSPIRE are the first.

articles.title: Gut microbiota as a potential mediator of the disease-ameliorating effects of molecular hydrogen: mechanisms and therapeutic perspectives.
articles.abstract: Molecular hydrogen (H2) has emerged as a promising bioactive gas with well-documented antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and cytoprotective properties, and its therapeutic potential for a range of human diseases has been increasingly recognized. Accumulating evidence suggests that the gut microbiota (GM) may contribute to some of the biological effects of H2. The GM serves as both a key site for endogenous H2 production and consumption, and a potential site of interaction with exogenous H2 supplementation, with possible implications for intestinal microecological homeostasis. This narrative review critically summarizes current evidence on the bidirectional relationship between H2 and the GM, focusing on microbial H2 production and consumption, the potential role of H2 in maintaining gut microbial homeostasis, and the impact of exogenous H2 supplementation on intestinal microecology. The potential therapeutic relevance of H2-associated GM modulation is further discussed in metabolic diseases, gastrointestinal disorders, and neurodegenerative diseases. Proposed mechanisms include regulation of microbial composition, reinforcement of intestinal barrier integrity, suppression of inflammation and oxidative stress, modulation of microbial metabolites, and gut-organ axis signaling. Collectively, current evidence supports that H2 may influence the GM ecosystem. However, most supporting data remains preclinical, and whether GM alterations causally mediate the biological or therapeutic effects of H2 remains to be established. Elucidating the reciprocal interaction between H2 and the GM may provide new mechanistic insight into H2-based interventions and facilitate the development of microbiota-targeted therapeutic strategies for human diseases.

articles.title: Phytochemical basis, multitarget pharmacology, and translational perspectives of silymarin: emphasis on its antifibrotic effects.
articles.abstract: This review critically evaluates the antifibrotic potential of silymarin by integrating its phytochemical composition, formulation-dependent exposure, molecular pharmacology, cross-organ preclinical evidence, and clinical translation, while distinguishing multicomponent silymarin extracts from purified silybin/silibinin and delivery-enhanced preparations. A structured, non-systematic evidence-mapping search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Scopus covered English-language literature through December 2025. A targeted update of PubMed/MEDLINE and publisher records was performed through 9 August 2026, focusing on fibrosis, pharmacokinetics, formulation, drug delivery, ferroptosis, succinate metabolism, ANXA6, and related mechanisms. Preclinical studies indicate that silymarin-related interventions can modulate TGF-β/Smad signaling, oxidative and inflammatory pathways, fibroblast activation, myofibroblast differentiation, and extracellular-matrix turnover. Recent work has added hepatocyte succinate handling, FTH1-related ferroptosis, and ANXA6-associated stress signaling. Antifibrotic activity has been reported in liver, kidney, lung, peritoneal, and skin models, whereas human evidence remains limited and heterogeneous. Product composition, oral exposure, formulation, and endpoint selection may contribute to discordant clinical findings. Silymarin has biologically plausible multitarget antifibrotic activity, but current evidence does not establish it as an antifibrotic therapy. Future studies should use chemically defined preparations, exposure-informed dosing, validated target engagement, and fibrosis-centered outcomes.

articles.title: COPD: real-world evidence on single-inhaler triple therapy and the emergence of biologic therapy.
articles.abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Despite major pharmacological advances, a substantial gap persists between guideline recommendations and routine clinical practice, particularly after exacerbations. This narrative review summarizes current evidence supporting personalized pharmacological escalation in COPD, focusing on single-inhaler triple therapy (SITT) and the emergence of biologic therapy. SITT, combining an inhaled corticosteroid, a long-acting β2-agonist and a long-acting muscarinic antagonist, is now the preferred inhaled strategy for patients requiring ICS-containing triple therapy. Real-world studies indicate that, compared with multiple-inhaler triple therapy, SITT is associated with better adherence and persistence, lower exacerbation rates and improved clinical outcomes, although observational findings require cautious causal interpretation. In parallel, COPD has entered the era of targeted biologic therapy. Dupilumab was the first biologic approved for COPD, following the BOREAS and NOTUS trials in patients with chronic bronchitis, blood eosinophils ≥300 cells/µL and persistent exacerbations despite triple therapy. Mepolizumab has more recently provided robust phase 3 evidence in eosinophilic COPD through the MATINEE trial. Early real-world dupilumab studies further suggest potential effectiveness in selected patients under-represented in pivotal trials, including those with advanced age, severe airflow limitation, oxygen dependence or high mucus burden. Beyond canonical type 2 pathways, IL-33 inhibition with tozorakimab may further broaden targeted treatment to COPD phenotypes without a clear eosinophilic signature. Integrating these advances within a treatable-traits framework may help optimize patient selection, close post-exacerbation therapeutic gaps, and align pharmacological escalation with comorbidity management, adherence, inhaler technique and rehabilitation needs.

articles.title: Chinese herbal medicine for recurrent urinary tract infection: formulation-specific clinical evidence, experimental pharmacology, and unresolved recurrence mechanisms.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Chinese herbal medicine (CHM) is used for recurrent or chronic urinary symptoms within the traditional category of dysuria, often through stage-specific treatment during symptomatic and remission phases. Whether defined CHM preparations prevent recurrent bacterial cystitis or modify recurrence biology remains uncertain. The aim of this study is to critically evaluate formulation-specific clinical evidence for CHM in women with recurrent urinary tract infection (rUTI) and determine whether reported benefits are connected to recurrence biology. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Structured searches of PubMed, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, and Wanfang Data were closed on 13 July 2026. After within-batch screening and cross-source reconciliation, 103 reports were linked into 96 study or unresolved-report clusters. Clusters were classified by directness, and clinical confidence was appraised using allocation, participant flow, recurrence ascertainment, denominator integrity, comparator, intervention identity, safety reporting, internal consistency, and report independence. RESULTS: Ten core clusters directly addressed prospective recurrence or suppressive treatment, but every comparative estimate was of very low confidence. Reported signals were formulation-specific and were limited by attrition, responder-conditioned denominators, active comparators, co-interventions, poorly defined recurrence, internal numerical inconsistencies, or report linkage. Botanical identity and study-batch chemistry were usually inadequate. Experimental studies supported anti-adhesion, virulence-modulating, anti-inflammatory, immune, and urothelial plausibility, including chemically characterized Persicaria capitata extract and more specific Caveolin-1 evidence for purified cynaroside, but predominantly used acute or pretreatment models. No microbiome or biomarker study evaluated clinical mediation. CONCLUSION: Current evidence is inconclusive rather than uniformly negative and supports cautious hypothesis generation for specific preparations, not a class-wide efficacy or safety claim. No clinical study demonstrates that CHM reduces recurrence by clearing persistent uropathogens, interrupting gut-bladder or vaginal transmission, restoring microbial ecology, or repairing the urothelial barrier. Reproducible products, intention-to-treat recurrence trials, longitudinal strain-resolved sampling, and prespecified mediation analyses are required.

articles.title: From cold chain to home care: emerging pharmaceutical challenges in monoclonal antibody therapy.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) are increasingly shifting from hospital intravenous infusion to subcutaneous self-administration at home, exposing fragile glycoproteins to thermal excursions, mechanical stress, and mishandling. These vulnerabilities are well documented in vitro and in preclinical models; however, their causal link to clinical treatment failure in home settings has not yet been established through prospective interventional or epidemiological studies. AREAS COVERED: This review examines the pharmaceutical challenges across the mAb lifecycle: degradation mechanisms, formulation strategies for high-concentration subcutaneous products (excipients, lyophilization, hyaluronidase-facilitated delivery), cold-chain vulnerabilities from manufacture to home storage, comparative analysis of intravenous versus subcutaneous administration, home-based practice challenges, and emerging technologies including IoT monitoring, smart packaging, and wearable injectors. Literature from pharmaceutical sciences, cold-chain engineering, device technology, and clinical practice (1974-2026) was synthesized. EXPERT OPINION: Ensuring mAb stability outside institutional walls requires an integrated four-pillar framework: mechanism-based formulation design, intelligent supply chain technologies, human-centered device engineering, and comprehensive patient education with digitally enabled professional support. While degradation mechanisms are well characterized, their translation into clinical outcomes in decentralized care remains an open research question. Future efforts should focus on thermostable formulations, validated temperature monitoring, intuitive delivery devices, and continuous care frameworks extending pharmaceutical expertise into patients' homes.

articles.title: Drug-toxin interactions in the brain: An overlooked dimension of psychopharmacology.
articles.abstract: This study aimed to suggest a new research field called 'environmental psychopharmacology' that will investigate the role of environmental chemical stressors in interfering with psychiatric drugs and in treatment resistance. This narrative review synthesizes knowledge on pharmacological, toxicological and environmental health data regarding the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic mechanisms involved in the action of psychotropic drugs, including blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, cytochrome P450 (CYP450) metabolism, P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux, neuroinflammation and mitochondrial oxidative stress. Environmental contaminants can affect the bioavailability of drugs in the central nervous system (CNS) by interfering with BBB integrity, changing the metabolism of the CYP450 family and increasing the activity of P-gp efflux pumps. A more complex picture may be presented, resulting in apparent 'pseudo-resistance' due to neuroinflammation and oxidative stress, which further diminishes drug-induced neuroplasticity. Drug-toxin interactions (DTIs) can occur either by direct interaction with a common molecular target or indirectly by modifying the biological environment. Bidirectional interactions between psychotropics and neurotoxic proteins may also be attributed to glymphatic clearance. Children, older adults and socio-economically disadvantaged groups are vulnerable populations. Environmental history-taking, toxicological screening and omics-based predictive modelling could become a powerful tool in the management of treatment-resistant psychiatric conditions.

articles.title: Assessing kidney function for drug dosing in critical illness.
articles.abstract: Kidney-function assessment supports drug dosing in critical illness but does not directly measure drug clearance. Reduced creatinine generation, fluid shifts and rapidly changing filtration can make creatinine-based estimates misleading, whereas genuinely augmented renal clearance can cause insufficient drug exposure. These processes can coexist. This narrative review distinguishes estimated glomerular filtration rate from estimated or measured creatinine clearance and explains how equation version, body-surface-area indexing and sampling time affect interpretation. It separates the 2021 creatinine, 2012 cystatin C and 2021 creatinine-cystatin C equations of the Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) and considers when each can inform a clinical decision. Cystatin C provides complementary information, not an intensive-care reference standard; timed urinary creatinine clearance is also vulnerable to collection error and changing physiology. We present a resource-adapted assessment framework rather than a validated dosing algorithm. It accommodates delayed cystatin C results, unavailable or unreliable urine collections, non-steady-state kidney function and access to therapeutic drug monitoring. Augmented renal clearance is treated as a continuum, with drug-specific thresholds distinguished from research definitions. Examples involving antibiotics, levetiracetam and gabapentin show why a kidney-function estimate must match the metric used in the relevant label or pharmacokinetic model. The practical objective is a documented, revisable dosing decision that integrates estimated kidney function, drug exposure and the consequences of under- or over-treatment, without assuming that biomarker discordance identifies its own cause.

articles.title: Adapting the WHO Global Competency Framework for Regulators of Medicines: Implementation lessons from the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority.
articles.abstract: AIMS: Medicines regulatory authorities require skilled staff to ensure timely, consistent and high-quality regulatory decision making. The World Health Organization Global Competency Framework (WHO-GCF) for Regulators of Medicines provides a common reference for defining regulatory workforce competencies while allowing adaptation to local needs. We describe the South African Health Products Regulatory Authority's (SAHPRA) implementation of the WHO-GCF and lessons learnt for other national regulatory authorities. METHODS: SAHPRA adapted the WHO-GCF through consultations with internal regulatory assessors, their supervisors and external experts. Activities, skills, responsibilities and competencies were reviewed for relevance and usability and adapted to reflect SAHPRA functions. The three WHO-GCF proficiency levels were expanded to four, informing revised assessor job profiles. The framework was implemented in a secure digital platform for self-assessment, supervisor validation and development planning. Graphical and summary reports were used to develop training and development plans at the team and individual levels. Hypothetical scenarios illustrate potential applications while protecting SAHPRA data confidentiality. RESULTS: The adapted framework retained the WHO-GCF domains relevant to SAHPRA with approximately 20% fewer competency statements. The laboratory analyst role was omitted, and SAHPRA-specific emphases such as biosimilar evaluation were added. Implementation challenges included assessment length, role specificity and the need to supplement ratings with evidence such as work samples. CONCLUSIONS: The WHO-GCF can be operationalized as an institution-specific framework while retaining a shared regulatory competency language. Local adaptation, involvement of frontline staff and evidence of competence are important for implementation. Competency frameworks can support targeted capacity building, reliance and work-sharing.

articles.title: "Nano-in-Gel Platforms for the Topical Treatment of Staphylococcus aureus Skin Infections".
articles.abstract: Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) is the leading cause of skin infections worldwide. Rising antimicrobial resistance limits the effectiveness of current treatments, highlighting the need for new therapeutic strategies. In this context, Rifabutin (RFB), could be repurposed for skin infections based on its strong anti-staphylococcal activity. However, its low oral bioavailability, and the rapid capacity of bacteria to develop drug tolerance, makes necessary to find novel platforms to ensure antimicrobial efficacy. This work proposes the development of Nano-in-Gel drug delivery systems, integrating RFB-loaded nanostructured lipid carriers (NLCs) into gelatin hydrogels for topical administration. These composite materials combine the controlled release capacity of hydrogels with NLCs´ ability to maximize RFB clinical potential. RFB-loaded NLCs were prepared and characterized in terms of physicochemical properties and cytocompatibility in human dermal fibroblasts (HDF). Moreover, their antibacterial activity against two different S. aureus strains-including mutants generated after RFB exposure was evaluated using a combination of conventional quantification methods and droplet digital PCR (ddPCR). Following the incorporation of NLCs into the gels, the mechanical properties of the Nano-in-Gel systems, and their ability to modulate nanoparticle release were assessed. Results demonstrated that the RFB-loaded NLCs possessed optimal physicochemical characteristics and high biocompatibility. Furthermore, the nanocarriers exhibited enhanced anti-staphylococcal activity compared to the free drug and successfully overcame RFB-resistance in mutant strains. The Nano-in-Gel platforms showed excellent mechanical performance for topical application and achieved a controlled NLCs release profile. These findings suggest that the Nano-in-Gel systems constitute a promising strategy for the advanced management of S. aureus skin infections.

articles.title: Reduced hypoxanthine Ameliorates LPS-triggered autism-like stereotyped behaviors in intestinal Tlr4 knockout mice via the DRN ROS-5-HT axis.
articles.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) involves social deficits and severe stereotyped behavior. While central serotonin (5-HT) systems and Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) activation are known to be implicated in ASD, how gut TLR4 affects central 5-HT and stereotyped behavior remains unknown. This study demonstrated that prenatal lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced social deficits in offspring of both intestinal Tlr4 knockout (Tlr4△IEC) and Tlr4fl/fl mice. However, the stereotyped behaviors and the inhibition of dorsal raphe nuclei (DRN) 5-HT were reduced in Tlr4△IEC-LPS mice compared with those in Tlr4fl/fl-LPS mice. By intersecting metabolites present in both colonic and cerebrospinal fluid, and selecting those exclusively changing in the colon of Tlr4fl/floffspring, hypoxanthine was identified as a metabolite that can cross the blood-brain barrier and mediate the effects of intestinal Tlr4 knockout on DRN 5-HT signaling. Remarkably, hypoxanthine and xanthine oxidase were increased in the serum of ASD children compared to typical development (TD) children. In vivo and in vitro experiments confirmed that hypoxanthine increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reduced 5-HT production, thereby promoting 5-HT neuron apoptosis. The inhibition of both the PI3K/AKT and 5-HT pathways in H2O2-treated PC12 cells was rescued by glutathione pretreatment in vitro. Meanwhile, the above LPS-induced DRN changes were significantly different in the Tlr4fl/fl offspring, and were reversed in the Tlr4△IEC mice after LPS exposure. Collectively, intestinal Tlr4 knockout reduces LPS-induced stereotyped behaviors, and the mechanism involves reduced hypoxanthine production and ROS-mediated inhibition of PI3K/AKT signaling, thereby decreasing 5-HT neuronal apoptosis by elevating the 5-HT level in DRN.

articles.title: Paeoniflorin Alleviates inflammatory injury in mastitis by targeting AKT1-Mediated mitochondrial damage and epithelial cell apoptosis.
articles.abstract: Peony can clear heat, promote blood circulation, and relieve pain, and peony-containing formulas exert favorable therapeutic effects on mastitis. Paeoniflorin is the primary bioactive component of peony. This study aimed to investigate the therapeutic targets and underlying mechanism of paeoniflorin (Pae) against mastitis, leveraging network pharmacology to guide experimental validation. A mouse mastitis model was established using lipopolysaccharide (LPS). Three concentrations of Pae were administered to evaluate its dose-dependent therapeutic effects, with dexamethasone (DXMS) serving as the positive control drug. Pae treatment significantly ameliorated mastitis in mice, reduced the expression of inflammatory cytokines, and alleviated cellular injury. Network pharmacology analysis revealed that AKT serine/threonine kinase 1 (AKT1) signaling was the most significantly enriched pathway, strongly correlated with both Pae and mastitis. Molecular dynamics simulation and CO-IP experiments confirmed the direct binding between Pae and AKT1. In vitro, we used bovine mammary epithelial cells, in which LPS was applied to induce inflammatory injury, to further verify the protective effects of Pae against cellular damage. The results showed that Pae protected against LPS-induced cellular injury in an AKT1-dependent manner. Mechanistically, Pae suppresses AKT1 phosphorylation and promotes AKT1 protein degradation. Collectively, through an integrated approach of network pharmacology and experimental validation, we identified that the therapeutic mechanism of Pae against mastitis is mediated by direct targeting of AKT1. Pae can bind to AKT1 and subsequently inhibit AKT1-mediated mitochondrial damage and epithelial apoptosis.

articles.title: Local transdermal delivery of Gallic acid using borneol-based transferosomes for enhanced breast cancer management.
articles.abstract: Local transdermal therapy (LTT) is a promising approach under investigation for breast cancer (BC) management. This approach primarily promotes the accumulation of the drug within breast tissue, rather than disseminating through the systemic circulation after topical application to the breast skin. Gallic acid (GA) is a versatile phenolic acid known for its antitumor activity. However, poor stability, degradation under alkaline conditions, oxidation sensitivity, and limited permeability restrict its therapeutic efficacy. Different transferosomes (TFs) were formulated via the thin film hydration method, and a D-optimal design was employed for their statistical analysis with respect to particle size (PS), polydispersity index (PDI), and entrapment efficiency (EE%). Moreover, to augment GA's skin penetration, penetration-enhanced transferosomes (PE-TFs) were prepared based on the optimized TFs. GA skin delivery was assessed through the evaluation of ex vivo skin permeation and deposition studies. The MTT assay was conducted to evaluate GA's antitumor activity. In vivo, an assessment of the selected formulations using 7,12-dimethylbenz[a]anthracene (DMBA)-induced BC was conducted. The PS, PDI, and EE% were 140 ± 1.17 nm, 0.25 ± 0.05, and 65% ± 5.51 for optimized TFs and 177.5 ± 2.38 nm, 0.291 ± 0.02, and 66% ± 1.81 for GA-borneol PE-TFs. The ex vivo permeation study demonstrated enhanced GA permeation from GA-borneol PE-TFs compared to the other tested formulations. The MTT assay indicated GA cytotoxic activity. Moreover, the GA-borneol PE-TFs gel demonstrated the highest percentage of drug retention, and in vivo studies emphasized its superiority in mitigating DMBA-induced BC during therapeutic and prophylactic studies.

articles.title: A multi-platform characterization of aggregation in morpholino oligonucleotide drug products: From soluble aggregates to subvisible particles.
articles.abstract: Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) represent a promising class of therapeutic agents; however, their efficacy and quality can be compromised by aggregation, a critical quality attribute that remains inadequately understood and analytically challenging. To address these methodological limitations, we evaluated the feasibility of both conventional and emerging analytical techniques for characterizing phosphorodiamidate morpholino oligomer (PMO) aggregates across their complete size distribution, from nanometer-scale soluble oligomers to micrometer-scale subvisible particles (SVP). Four FDA-approved PMO drug products were analyzed using five complementary methods selected to cover distinct size ranges: flow imaging (FI) microscopy for SVP (3-100 μm), microfluidic resistive pulse sensing (MRPS) for submicron particles (250-2000 nm), size-exclusion chromatography with multi-angle light scattering (SEC-MALS) and asymmetric flow field-flow fractionation (AF4) for soluble aggregates, and intact mass spectrometry for rapid qualitative assessment of noncovalent assemblies. Method performance, recovery, and orthogonality were systematically evaluated. Additionally, we assessed the effectiveness of filtration (0.2 μm and 0.02 μm) as a risk mitigation strategy and examined the impact of product age on aggregation extent. Aggregates were detected across all size ranges in all four marketed PMO products, with substantial product-specific variability in both quantity and size distribution. SEC-MALS achieved >80% recovery and detected oligomeric species ranging from dimers to tetramers, with soluble aggregate levels ranging from 0.27% to 6.75% for the products tested. MRPS quantified submicron particles at concentrations exceeding 10⁵ particles/mL, while FI detected SVP concentrations ranging from 129 to 3,544 particles/mL. These PMO aggregates exhibited moderate transparency (transparency < 0.6), suggesting potential undercounting by traditional light obscuration methods. AF4 and intact mass spectrometry-applied here for the first time to PMOs-confirmed the presence of high molecular weight species, although AF4 separation of monomers and dimers was incomplete for some products. Intact mass spectrometry enabled direct detection of noncovalent aggregates without chromatographic separation. Assessment of product stability revealed that expired products exhibited up to a 1,000-fold increase in particle burden compared to products within shelf life. Evaluation of filtration as a control strategy demonstrated that 0.2 μm filtration reduced SVP by >95% while leaving soluble aggregates unaffected. This multi-platform analytical approach enables comprehensive characterization of PMO aggregation spanning from nanometer to micrometer scales. The current study provides analytical scientists with enhanced understanding of analytical technologies for subvisible particles measurements which may be selected as part of a control strategy and used to monitor this critical quality attribute in oligonucleotide therapeutic during development and manufacturing.

articles.title: The impact of perceived volume limits on subcutaneous biologic drug development: an industry survey.
articles.abstract: As multiple large-volume subcutaneous (SC) biologics enter trials or gain approval, understanding how administration volume impacts biologic development is critical. While patients often prefer SC over intravenous administration, large-volume SC delivery adoption is hindered by the belief that SC delivery must be ≤3 mL without a permeation enhancer (PE). A 21-item online survey was conducted among professionals working in research and development; chemistry, manufacturing, and controls (CMC); portfolio strategy, new product planning; and combination products. Questions explored perceptions of SC administration volume limits, biologic deprioritization and abandonment, large-volume delivery considerations, and organizational approaches to revisiting deprioritized candidates. Eighty-eight participants completed the survey; 90.9% reported direct involvement in at least one project in which a biologic had been deprioritized or abandoned due to challenges achieving an SC volume of ≤3 mL. Respondents estimated that a weighted mean of 32.4% of relevant biologics had been abandoned and 28.9% had been deprioritized because of such challenges. Frequently selected reasons included limited experience with large-volume formulations or devices (29.5%), patient and/or healthcare provider preference (19.3%), and development costs or timelines (17.0%). Overall, 33.0% of respondents selected ≤3 mL as the maximum volume for SC infusion over several minutes without a PE. These findings indicate that perceived SC volume constraints may influence development decisions and highlight the importance of differentiating between device-related and physiological limits on SC administration volume. This study demonstrates that misconceptions about SC injection volume limits may lead to deprioritization or abandonment of viable assets during biologic development.

articles.title: Cell-penetrating peptide functionalized ZIF-90 platform for photodynamic-chemical combined therapy in colorectal cancer.
articles.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the major concerns of developed nations. The combination of different treatment modalities has been shown to be effective in improving tumor therapy efficiency and reducing side effects. However, the synergistic anti-tumor efficiency and highly responsive drug release still remain challenging. Curcumin (CCM) has a chemotherapeutic effect as well as significant photodynamic activity, which is a promising component for the treatment of tumors. Herein, we report a cell-penetrating peptide functionalized ZIF-90-based drug delivery platform (PEG-CPP2@NPs) for synergistic photodynamic-chemical combined therapy in colorectal cancer. Polyethylene glycol (PEG)-conjugated CPP2 coating obviously increased the uptake of nanoparticles in tumor cells and their accumulation in tumor tissues. We conducted in vivo and in vitro experiments to evaluate the anti-tumor effects of CCM-loaded multifunctional nanoparticles. The PEG-CPP2@NPs exhibited significant tumor inhibition. After laser irradiation treatment, the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), mitochondrial damage, and cell apoptosis, as well as the expressions of Bax/Bcl-2, cytochrome C, and caspase-3, were all significantly enhanced. The tumor suppression rates in mice across the treatment groups were 25.46% for CCM, 33.16% for NPs, 43.5% for CCM+L, 48.45% for NPs+L, 66.05% for PEG-CPP2@NPs, and 80.64% for PEG-CPP2@NPs+L. This indicates that the functionalized ZIF-90 platform, when combined with chemotherapy and photodynamic therapy, has a stronger anti-tumor effect. Overall, the novel drug-delivery platform designed herein has demonstrated significant potential in the treatment of colon cancer and has provided a new approach for enhancing anti-tumor efficacy.

articles.title: Effects of maternal exposure to 2,6-dichloro-1,4-benzoquinone during pregnancy and lactation on the gut microbiota and neurodevelopment in offspring rats.
articles.abstract: 2,6-dichloro-1,4-benzoquinone (DCBQ), as an emerging drinking water disinfection byproduct, has been widely detected in drinking water and pose potential risks. However, there are relatively few reports on their potential neurodevelopmental toxicity, especially the lack of in vivo studies as the most direct evidence. A rat model was established for the entire gestation and lactation period to study the neurodevelopmental toxicity of DCBQ in offspring rats, through evaluating gut microbiota, neurotransmitters and neurobehaviors. Maternal rats were administered with DCBQ at 0.5, 5, and 50 mg/kg body weight via gavage throughout gestation and lactation. Our results showed that maternal DCBQ exposure induced prolonged neural reflex behavior, decreased motor activity, and increased anxiety-like behavior in offspring rats. And the levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factors and neurotransmitters, especially glutamate and dopamine, in serum and hippocampus were significantly decreased in offspring rats after maternal DCBQ exposure. Maternal DCBQ exposure induced imbalance of intestinal microbiota in a gender-specific way.
