In addition, maternal DCBQ exposure induced significant changes of 123 metabolites, affecting multiple metabolic pathways, such as mTOR pathway. In particular, the altered gut microbiota showed strong associations with altered metabolites, neurotransmitters and neurobehaviors after maternal DCBQ exposure. Our findings suggest that maternal DCBQ exposure may impair neurodevelopment and disrupt gut microbiota and fecal metabolite profiles of offspring rats, indicating a potential gut microbiota-metabolome-neurochemical link. Our study highlights the importance of evaluating the neurodevelopmental toxicity of disinfection byproducts in future.

articles.title: SP1-CD44 signaling modulates PPP-associated metabolism and gemcitabine sensitivity in pancreatic cancer cells.
articles.abstract: Gemcitabine (GEM) resistance poses a significant challenge to the survival of patients with pancreatic cancer. A key mechanism underlying this resistance is the aberrant activation of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), which leads to increased levels of deoxycytidine triphosphate (dCTP) and competitively inhibits the incorporation of gemcitabine into DNA. However, the upstream regulator of PPP hyperactivation in GEM-resistant pancreatic cancer remains unclear. Here, we reported that SP1-CD44 signaling modulated gemcitabine sensitivity and PPP-associated metabolic parameters in pancreatic cancer. Mechanistically, knockdown of SP1 reduced G6PDH activity and decreased the levels of NADPH and G6P, whereas overexpression of CD44 resulted in the opposite effects. Functionally, inhibition of this axis increased the sensitivity of pancreatic cancer cells to GEM. Given its therapeutic potential, we sought to identify candidate SP1-targeting compounds with the potential to enhance gemcitabine sensitivity. A small-scale screen of known SP1 inhibitors revealed mithramycin A (MIT) to be effective, but its significant toxicity is well documented. To identify safer alternatives, we screened anti‑pancreatic cancer natural products in the natural product library of our laboratory, guided by computer-aided drug discovery. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations suggested that arenobufagin (ABA) and bufalin (BA) may bind to SP1. In summary, our findings support a role for the SP1-CD44 axis in gemcitabine resistance and suggest that enhanced PPP-associated metabolic activity may contribute to this phenotype. Furthermore, we identified ABA and BA as candidate compounds that increase gemcitabine-associated apoptosis in pancreatic cancer cells, warranting further investigation of their potential as SP1-targeting agents.

articles.title: Cardiomyocyte-derived ACE2/Ang-(1-7) axis mediates DIZE-induced inhibition of TGF-β signaling to attenuate cardiac fibrosis following myocardial infarction.
articles.abstract: Cardiac fibrosis represents a critical pathological determinant of poor prognosis in coronary artery disease (CAD). Pharmacological activation of the angiotensin-Converting enzyme 2/angiotensin-(1-7) (ACE2/Ang-(1-7)) axis is a promising anti-fibrotic approach for cardiac fibrosis, a condition that currently lacks effective therapies. Diminazene aceturate (DIZE) is recognized as an ACE2 agonist with anti‑fibrotic activity, the molecular mechanism of which has not been fully elucidated. This study demonstrates that the anti-fibrotic effects of DIZE are exerted via a cardiomyocyte-mediated paracrine mechanism, rather than through direct action on fibroblasts. Using a cardiomyocyte-fibroblast co-culture system and transcriptomic analysis, we found that ACE2 activated by DIZE on cardiomyocytes enhances the conversion of Ang II to Ang-(1-7), which subsequently suppresses the pro-fibrotic transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β) signaling in adjacent fibroblasts. This effect was partially abrogated by the Ang-(1-7) antagonist A779, confirming Ang-(1-7) as a key paracrine mediator. To exploit this mechanism in vivo, a collagen-binding, low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU)-responsive nanoplatform (CNA35-GDP) was developed for specific DIZE delivery. In a rat model of myocardial infarction, LIFU-triggered DIZE release from CNA35-GDP was found to significantly improve cardiac function and attenuate fibrosis. These therapeutic benefits were accompanied by restoration of the ACE2/Ang-(1-7) axis and suppression of TGF-β signaling, thereby validating the proposed mechanism. Collectively, activation of cardiomyocyte-derived ACE2 by DIZE inhibits collagen production in fibroblasts through paracrine Ang-(1-7) and downstream suppression of TGF‑β signaling.

articles.title: GPR146 as a therapeutic target: Linking lipid metabolism with macrophage inflammation in atherosclerosis.
articles.abstract: Atherosclerosis is driven by dyslipidemia and chronic inflammation. GPR146 has emerged as a regulator of cholesterol metabolism; however, whether GPR146 links lipid metabolism with macrophage inflammation during atherosclerosis remains unclear. Apolipoprotein E-deficient (ApoE-/-) mice were fed a high-fat diet for 12 weeks, followed by 4 weeks of intervention with adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated hepatic GPR146 knockdown or rosuvastatin treatment. Atherosclerotic lesions and plaque composition were assessed using Oil Red O staining and immunofluorescence. Lipid profiles, oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL), and inflammatory markers were evaluated using enzymatic assays, ELISA, and qPCR, respectively. In ox-LDL-stimulated THP-1-derived macrophages, GPR146 was silenced to examine lipid accumulation, inflammatory responses, transcriptomic alterations, and the potential involvement of the JAK-STAT signaling pathway. GPR146 expression increased in atherosclerotic lesions, particularly in macrophage-rich regions. Hepatic GPR146 knockdown reduced atherosclerotic lesion burden, circulating total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels, ox-LDL accumulation, and inflammatory activation within plaques. In macrophages, GPR146 silencing suppressed ox-LDL-induced lipid accumulation, accompanied by reduced CD36 expression and decreased foam cell formation. GPR146 silencing also attenuated pro-inflammatory macrophage activation, as evidenced by reduced expression of inflammatory mediators. Transcriptomic analysis implicated JAK-STAT signaling, with reduced JAK2 and STAT3 expression following GPR146 silencing. Pharmacological inhibition of the JAK-STAT signaling partially recapitulated the anti-inflammatory effects associated with GPR146 knockdown. Together, these findings suggest that GPR146 contributes to lipid metabolic regulation and macrophage inflammatory responses during atherosclerosis and may represent a therapeutic target warranting further investigation.

articles.title: A defect-free nanofiber is not yet a medicine: The translational debt of pharmaceutical electrospinning.
articles.abstract: Pharmaceutical electrospinning increasingly enables sophisticated drug-loaded architectures, yet structural innovation does not necessarily translate into clinically or industrially viable medicines. This Commentary introduces complexity-induced translational debt as a conceptual lens for considering the incremental manufacturing, analytical, stability, pharmacokinetic, usability, and scale-up obligations created by added architectural, compositional, or process complexity. We propose that added complexity be considered in relation to the therapeutic or product-level value it is intended to provide, ideally against an appropriate simpler comparator. Two complementary principles are proposed: minimum sufficient complexity, which favors the least complex design capable of meeting the intended product requirements, and complexity-evidence-control alignment, which considers whether the evidence and control strategy are commensurate with the complexity and claims introduced. Representative studies illustrate how added complexity may be justified, incompletely supported, or outweighed by manufacturability considerations. A product-centered development strategy integrating exposure evidence, pharmaceutical quality attributes, and process control may help shift electrospun systems from elegant laboratory constructs toward reproducible drug products with credible therapeutic, manufacturing, and translational value in practice.

articles.title: Extended Clopidogrel Monotherapy versus Dual Antiplatelet Therapy in Acute Coronary Syndrome Patients With and Without Heart Failure: A Prespecified Subgroup Analysis of the OPT-BIRISK Trial.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The optimal extended antiplatelet strategy after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for acute coronary syndrome (ACS) in patients with heart failure (HF) remains uncertain. METHODS: In OPT-BIRISK, patients at high ischemic and bleeding risk who completed 9-12 months of dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) were randomized to clopidogrel plus placebo or aspirin for 9 months. This analysis compared treatments by recorded HF history. The primary endpoint was Bleeding Academic Research Consortium (BARC) types 2, 3, or 5 bleeding; the key secondary endpoint was major adverse cardiac and cerebral events (MACCE). RESULTS: Of 7,758 patients, 653 (8.4%) had HF history. Without HF, bleeding occurred in 83/3,565 (2.3%) monotherapy recipients and 118/3,540 (3.3%) DAPT recipients (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.53-0.92). With HF, bleeding occurred in 12/308 (3.9%) and 9/345 (2.6%), respectively (HR 1.49, 95% CI 0.63-3.53). MACCE occurred in 90/3,565 (2.5%) versus 120/3,540 (3.4%) patients without HF (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.57-0.98) and 11/308 (3.6%) versus 16/345 (4.6%) patients with HF (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.36-1.66). Interaction P values were 0.1021 for bleeding and 0.9345 for MACCE. CONCLUSIONS: Extended clopidogrel monotherapy reduced clinically relevant bleeding in patients without a history of HF after PCI for ACS. No statistically significant treatment-by-HF interaction was observed for bleeding or MACCE, although HF-specific treatment effects remain inconclusive because of limited events.

articles.title: Snake venom toxin-inspired peptide AMPAB5 combats multidrug-resistant bacteria and suppresses inflammatory responses in human cells.
articles.abstract: Snake venom toxin-inspired peptides represent a promising source of multifunctional antimicrobial agents. This study evaluates AMPAB5, a new synthetic peptide engineered from cobra (Naja ashei) venom factor sequences, targeting wound-associated pathogens, especially multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus, as well as Klebsiella pneumoniae and Staphylococcus epidermidis. In particular, AMPAB5 significantly inhibits the formation and eradicates P. aeruginosa biofilms, which is of high clinical importance. Despite intrinsic chloramphenicol resistance of P. aeruginosa (MIC = 250.00 μg/mL) the combination of the antibiotic with AMPAB5 resulted in a 16-fold potentiation, reducing the MICs to 15.63 μg/mL for chloramphenicol and 5.86 μg/mL for the peptide. This significant drop directly reflects the mutual enhancement of both antibacterial agents, highlighting their synergistic effect. Mechanistic studies revealed that the peptide enhances permeability of the bacterial membrane, promoting the efficacy of chloramphenicol. Furthermore, AMPAB5 exhibits potent anti-inflammatory activities by modulating the secretion of IL-1β and TNF-α cytokines by human macrophages. Additionally, the free peptide demonstrated excellent biocompatibility, lack of hemolytic activity and no cytotoxicity against human keratinocytes (HaCaT) or adenocarcinoma cells (Caco-2). These findings demonstrate that AMPAB5 is a highly biosafe dual-action therapeutic candidate capable of eradicating resilient microbial biofilm infections while mitigating host inflammation in chronic wounds.

articles.title: Milu antler powder demonstrates efficacy in mitigating kidney damage induced by the aging process through the modulation of intestinal microbiota.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Aging significantly affects the structure and function of the kidney, leading to profound changes. Ancient texts document that deer antler powder can ameliorate renal damage and aging, but its exact mechanism of action remains unclear. AIM OF STUDY: To evaluate the renal protective capabilities of Milu antler powder in senescent mice and elucidate its mechanism of action in alleviating renal injury. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We prepared and conducted the ultramicro-grade Milu antler powder (UGM) and evaluated its effectiveness in improving kidney function in D-galactose-induced senescent mice through biochemical indices and histological studies. We then employed UPLC-MS/MS and 16S rRNA gene analysis to analyze the changes in intestinal microbiota and metabolites. Finally, the effects of UGM and its metabolites on the aging phenotype and renal function in mice were verified through fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) and cell experiments. RESULTS: UGM significantly ameliorated brain aging and immune decline in senescent mice. Notably, it significantly reduced renal structural damage and aging phenotype, and improved renal dysfunction. The 16S rRNA gene analysis and its metabolite analyses showed that UGM was able to upregulate Akkermansia, Lachnospiraceae_NK4A136_group and downregulate Desulfobacterota, as well as alter metabolite expression (especially sodium acetate). Furthermore, through FMT and HK-2 cell experiments, we confirmed that Milu antler powder was able to attenuate renal aging by modulating the intestinal microbiota and their metabolites (sodium acetate). CONCLUSIONS: This study provides a scientific basis for the anti-aging application of Milu antler powder by demonstrating its ability to attenuate renal aging through modulation of the gut-kidney axis.

articles.title: Total alkaloids from Sophora flavescens and Sophora flavescens film ameliorate intrauterine adhesions in rats with associated changes in IL-17A/MMP-related inflammatory and fibrotic responses.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Sophora flavescens Aiton has been used in various traditional medical systems in East Asia, including Miao medicine in China, for conditions described as heat-related, parasitic, urinary, and gynecological disorders. Its quinolizidine alkaloids have reported anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic activities, providing an ethnopharmacological rationale for investigating their potential relevance to endometrial injury and fibrosis associated with intrauterine adhesions (IUA). AIM OF THE STUDY: To evaluate the effects of oral total alkaloids from Sophora flavescens (TASF) combined with intrauterine application of Sophora flavescens film (SFF) in a rat model of IUA and to explore mechanisms. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A rat model of IUA was established by mechanical endometrial injury combined with inflammatory stimulation. Rats received combined oral TASF and intrauterine SFF (TASF-SFF). TASF constituents and plasma-associated compounds were profiled using UPLC-MS/MS. An HPLC method was established and validated for the quantification of four major alkaloids in TASF and SFF separately. Histological evaluation and marker expression analysis were performed using H&E and Masson staining alongside RT-qPCR, Western blotting, and ELISA. Transcriptomics and network pharmacology screened key pathways. RESULTS: Thirty constituents were identified in TASF, with matrine and oxymatrine as predominant compounds. The combined treatment regimens were associated with reduced endometrial injury and collagen deposition and with changes in implantation outcomes and endometrial receptivity-associated markers. Transcriptomics and network pharmacology prioritized IL-17 signaling as a candidate pathway. Treatment was accompanied by changes in IL-17A, IL-17RA, TRAF6, NF-κB/MAPK phosphorylation, and MMP-3/MMP-9 expression. CONCLUSION: TASF-SFF combination treatment alleviated endometrial inflammation and fibrosis and improved endometrial receptivity-related indicators in a rat model of IUA. These effects were associated with changes in IL-17/MMP-related signaling, suggesting its potential involvement in the treatment response.

articles.title: Astragalus membranaceus-derived exosomes deliver calycosin to orchestrate the Nrf2/SLC7A11/GPX4 axis against ferroptosis in Parkinson's disease.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Astragalus membranaceus (Fisch.) Bunge (Fabaceae) is documented in Shennong's Classic of Materia Medica to treat Qi deficiency-induced cerebral blood stasis and limb tremor resembling Parkinson's disease (PD). Its primary bioactive component, calycosin (CA), exerts anti-ferroptosis effects; however, its ability to cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB) is severely limited. Herbal-derived exosomes isolated from Astragalus membranaceus act as homologous natural nanocarriers to overcome this limitation; however, the anti-PD efficacy and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2)-dependent ferroptosis regulatory mechanism of Astragalus membranaceus-derived exosomes (AS-Exos) loaded with CA (AS-Exos-CA) remain unelucidated. AIM OF THE STUDY: To construct AS-Exos-CA, verify both its BBB-crossing capacity and neuroprotective effect on dopaminergic neurons, and investigate whether its anti-ferroptosis protection relies on the Nrf2/SLC7A11/GPX4 axis, to provide modern pharmacological evidence for the ethnopharmacological application of Astragalus membranaceus against PD. MATERIALS AND METHODS: AS-Exos were isolated by ultracentrifugation and characterized using NTA and TEM. HPLC was employed to screen the optimal CA-loading ratio for preparing AS-Exos-CA and measure its encapsulation efficiency. PKH26 and DiR fluorescence labeling were used to assess cellular uptake and BBB penetration of AS-Exos-CA in PC12 cells and 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP)-induced mice, respectively. Motor function, dopaminergic neuron survival, ferroptosis-related oxidative stress, iron metabolism and mitochondrial ultrastructure were assessed to evaluate the therapeutic effects of AS-Exos-CA in MPTP-induced PD mice. 1-methyl-4-phenylpyridinium ion (MPP+)-injured PC12 cells combined with the Nrf2-specific inhibitor ML385 were used to verify the Nrf2-dependent mechanism mediating AS-Exos-CA-derived protection. RESULTS: AS-Exos-CA displayed typical vesicle morphology, was efficiently taken up by PC12 cells, and significantly accumulated in mouse brain 12 h after intravenous injection. Compared with free CA and AS-Exos, AS-Exos-CA more effectively ameliorated motor deficits, rescued dopaminergic neurons, mitigated mitochondrial injury and iron deposition, restored glutathione (GSH), and lowered malondialdehyde (MDA) and reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels. AS-Exos-CA facilitated Nrf2 nuclear translocation and up-regulated the downstream expression of SLC7A11 and GPX4. ML385 abolished its in vitro anti-ferroptotic actions, verifying the essential role of Nrf2 signaling. CONCLUSION: AS-Exos serve as homologous herbal nanocarriers, enhancing CA penetration across the BBB for brain delivery. AS-Exos-CA exerts robust neuroprotection against PD largely by inhibiting neuronal ferroptosis via the Nrf2/SLC7A11/GPX4 pathway. This herbal exosome-based nanoformulation overcomes the biocompatibility limitations of synthetic nanomaterials and represents a promising disease-modifying strategy for PD, thereby advancing the modern investigation of Qi-tonifying herbal medicines in degenerative central nervous system (CNS) disorders.

articles.title: Prediction of human intestinal passive membrane permeability using physiologically informed machine learning models.
articles.abstract: Predicting human intestinal passive membrane permeability (Peff) is essential for reliable application of physiologically based biopharmaceutics models (PBBMs). Although in vitro cell-based assays and animal studies are widely used, their predictive performance is often limited by inter-laboratory variability and species differences. Furthermore, accurate prediction of intrinsic permeability requires consideration of physiological factors, particularly correction for the unstirred water layer (UWL) and exclusion of transporter-mediated transport. We developed machine learning models to predict human jejunal Peff directly from chemical structure using a physiologically curated dataset derived from in vivo human jejunal permeability data. The dataset was refined by excluding transporter substrates and correcting for UWL resistance to estimate intrinsic cellular permeability (Pcell). To maximize predictive performance while maintaining robustness with a limited dataset, two feature selection strategies were evaluated: a data-driven approach to identify novel structure-permeability relationships and a hypothesis-driven approach based on established physicochemical principles. The practical applicability of the developed models was assessed by incorporating the predicted Peff values into a PBBM. The data-driven model demonstrated superior generalization performance and accurately reproduced observed human plasma concentration-time profiles. These findings demonstrate that the proposed approach can robustly predict intrinsic human intestinal membrane permeability from chemical structure alone.

articles.title: A novel in-vitro skin model to assess secondary transfer of applied testosterone following skin to skin contact.
articles.abstract: Transdermal testosterone gels are popular and widely used for testosterone replacement therapy. However, unintended exposure of other individuals to testosterone through secondary transfer of the product caused by skin-to-skin contact is a recognised risk with their use. Case reports have described children developing clinical symptoms following inadvertent transfer, despite controlled in vivo studies generally suggesting that secondary transfer is minimal once the gel has dried. At present, there is limited consensus regarding the guidance patients should follow to minimise transfer risk, and regulatory agencies have highlighted the need for an in vitro model capable of investigating transfer mechanisms and mitigation strategies. In this study, an in vitro model was developed to evaluate the influence of the time interval between gel application and skin-to-skin contact on testosterone transfer and absorption, as well as the impact of sweat on these processes. The model was based on the Franz diffusion cell system and simulated controlled skin-to-skin contact between 'primary' skin, representing the treated individual, and 'secondary' skin, representing the exposed individual. Experiments were conducted using both porcine and human skin following application of Testogel to the primary skin surface. As expected, the lowest transfer of testosterone to secondary skin occurred when contact was made after the testosterone film had fully dried, with a 7-fold reduction in transferred testosterone compared to when contact was made immediately after dosing. This resulted in a 14-fold reduction in testosterone absorption into the secondary skin. However, although the greatest amount of testosterone remained on the primary skin under fully dried conditions, skin-to-skin contact at this stage resulted in a 2-fold reduction in testosterone absorption into the primary skin itself. This effect has not previously been reported. Raman microscopy demonstrated that this reduction was associated with disruption of intimate contact between the dried testosterone film and the primary skin following skin-to-skin contact, suggesting that such contact may also compromise therapeutic efficacy. In the presence of sweat, secondary transfer and absorption were increased approximately 5-fold and 3-fold, respectively, compared with contact in the absence of sweat, demonstrating for the first time the important role of perspiration in enhancing transfer risk. Overall, the developed model provided new mechanistic insight into factors governing secondary transfer and absorption from topical hormonal products and represents a promising approach to support formulation development and reduce the need for in vivo clinical studies.

articles.title: Liposomal delivery of triptolide fatty acid prodrugs with varied fatty acid chain lengths for breast cancer therapy.
articles.abstract: Triptolide is a highly potent natural antitumor agent whose clinical translation has been limited by systemic toxicity, narrow therapeutic window, and insufficient formulation stability. To address these limitations from a formulation-oriented perspective, a liposomal platform based on fatty acid-conjugated triptolide prodrugs was developed to investigate how fatty acid chain length influences formulation and plasma conversion behavior. Triptolide was covalently linked to myristic (C14), palmitic (C16), stearic (C18), eicosanoic (C20), and behenic (C22) acids and subsequently formulated into liposomal systems using a thin-film hydration method. The physicochemical properties were characterized, and plasma conversion, cytotoxicity, local irritation, and in vivo antitumor activity were evaluated. The free TP-FA prodrugs and their corresponding liposomal formulations exhibited distinct plasma conversion profiles. At 48 h, free TP-SA, TP-EA, and TP-BA showed conversion percentages of 97.53%, 97.02%, and 97.21%, respectively, whereas the corresponding liposomal formulations showed conversion percentages of 90.96%, 80.31%, and 41.83%, respectively. The difference between the free and liposomal forms was more persistent for the longer-chain conjugates, although the relationship with fatty acid chain length was not strictly monotonic across all time points. Among the tested formulations, behenic acid-conjugated liposomes showed distinct plasma conversion behavior and were further evaluated in the local irritation and in vivo antitumor studies. These findings suggest that saturated fatty acid chain length represents one structural variable influencing the behavior of TP-FA liposomal formulations.

articles.title: Bisdemethoxycurcumin disrupts Chk1-associated DNA damage checkpoint signaling and induces apoptosis in nasopharyngeal carcinoma cells.
articles.abstract: Curcuminoids have been widely explored for their diverse bioactivities, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antitumor effects. Among them, bisdemethoxycurcumin (BDMC) has been reported to suppress tumor proliferation and metastasis in several cancer types. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying the effects of BDMC in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) remain unclear. The effects of BDMC on apoptosis, cell-cycle progression, DNA damage, and Chk1 activity were examined using immunoblotting, flow cytometry, immunocytochemistry, and cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA). Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations were performed using BIOVIA Discovery Studio 2024. Our results demonstrated that BDMC exerted cytotoxic effects by inducing both intrinsic and extrinsic apoptotic pathways in NPC cells. c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) signaling was involved in apoptotic induction through suppression of JNK phosphorylation. In parallel, BDMC directly engaged checkpoint kinase 1 (Chk1) and inhibited its phosphorylation. Chk1 inhibition by BDMC led to disruption of checkpoint control, S- and G2/M-phase arrest, and accumulation of DNA damage, accompanied by a distinct inactivation of Chk1 phosphorylation without alteration of total Chk1 protein expression. Notably, CHEK1 silencing did not significantly alter BDMC-induced caspase activation or apoptosis, whereas inhibition of caspase-dependent apoptosis with Z-VAD did not affect BDMC-induced γH2AX accumulation. These findings suggest that the apoptotic response and the Chk1-associated DNA damage response induced by BDMC are functionally separable under the conditions examined. This study reveals that the antitumor effects of BDMC involve distinct modulation of JNK-associated apoptotic signaling and Chk1-mediated checkpoint dysfunction. These findings provide mechanistic insight into BDMC-induced cytotoxicity and support its potential as a lead compound for further pharmacological investigation in NPC.

articles.title: The impact of GLP-1 receptor agonists on chemotherapeutic efficacy: insights from GWAS and experiments.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Emerging evidence highlights the anti-tumor properties of Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs). However, their synergistic potential with standard chemotherapy remains largely unexplored. METHODS: Data from Genome-wide association study (GWAS) were used to select single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) strongly associated with lipid-lowering drug targets as instrumental variables. Causal effects were assessed primarily using the inverse variance weighted (IVW) method, supported by comprehensive sensitivity analyses to control for pleiotropy and heterogeneity. These Mendelian randomization (MR) findings were further validated through in vitro functional assays (cell viability, apoptosis, and Western blot) and an in vivo tumor-bearing mouse model. RESULTS: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) activity showed a significantly positive causal relationship with dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR; β = 0.323, P = 6.02 × 10-17) and apoptosis regulator Bcl-2 (β = 0.259, P = 2.1 × 10-11) but a negative relationship with ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase large subunit (RRM1; β = -0.12, P = 2.32 × 10-3). Functional experiments validated these genetic findings. GLP-1RA significantly enhanced the antitumoral efficacy of gemcitabine both in vitro and in vivo by repressing RRM1. Conversely, GLP-1RA attenuated the anti-tumor effects of methotrexate and paclitaxel by upregulating DHFR and Bcl-2, respectively. Notably, GLP-1RA combination therapy achieved these modulatory effects without exacerbating chemotherapy-associated systemic toxicity. CONCLUSION: GLP1-RAs can influence the efficacy of chemotherapeutic drugs such as methotrexate, paclitaxel, and gemcitabine.

articles.title: Dementia-related risk associated with endocrine and targeted therapy strategies in breast cancer: a real-world pharmacovigilance analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: In clinical practice, adjuvant endocrine and targeted (ET) therapy strategies for hormone receptor-positive (HR+) breast cancer are constantly evolving. The long-term cognitive impact of such adjuvant treatment on patients remains unclear. METHODS: This study mined data from the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) from 2010Q1 to 2025Q2 to examine the relationship between ET therapy strategies and adverse events (AEs) related to dementia. Standardized Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) Queries (SMQs) containing "broad" and "narrow" preferred terms (PTs) for dementia were used to systematically identify AE reports associated with dementia. The disproportionality analysis was conducted using the Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean (EBGM) calculated by the Multi-Item Gamma Poisson Shrinker (MGPS) and the proportional reporting ratio together with chi-square (PRR, χ2). RESULTS: As a whole, risk signals are negative in narrow or broad dementia (narrow: EBGM05 1.27, PRR 1.32 [χ2 5.75]; broad: EBGM05 1.02, PRR 1.03 [χ2 2.88]). In subgroup analyses, positive signals of narrow dementia were identified for anastrozole monotherapy (n = 20, EBGM05 4.00, PRR 4.68 [χ2 53.20]) and exemestane monotherapy (n = 9, EBGM05 2.10, PRR 2.64 [χ2 8.85]) in female adult breast cancer cases, as well as for anastrozole monotherapy in reporters over 50 years old (n = 20, EBGM05 2.52, PRR 3.67 [χ2 39.87]). CONCLUSION: This FAERS-based pharmacovigilance analysis identifies subgroup-specific narrow-spectrum dementia safety signals for aromatase inhibitor monotherapy in breast cancer patients, most notably anastrozole in women aged over 50 years. These hypothesis-generating observations warrant prospective validation.

articles.title: Ginsenoside RK3 suppresses osteosarcoma via PRMT5/GPX4-ferroptosis axis and enhances doxorubicin chemosensitivity.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Osteosarcoma (OS), the most common primary malignant bone tumor in children and adolescents, commonly develops chemoresistance to conventional apoptosis-dependent therapies (e.g., doxorubicin) in metastatic/recurrent settings, leading to poor prognosis. Ferroptosis-an iron-dependent cell death pathway driven by lipid peroxidation-offers a promising alternative, yet clinical translation of synthetic inducers is limited by poor druggability. PURPOSE: This study systematically investigates the antitumor efficacy of ginsenoside RK3 in OS, explores its potential involvement in the PRMT5/GPX4-ferroptosis axis, and evaluates its potential as a doxorubicin chemosensitizer. METHODS: Antitumor effects of RK3 were assessed in MG63/U2OS cells and OS xenografts. Mechanisms were explored through bioinformatics, molecular docking, co-immunoprecipitation, and ubiquitination assays. The combinatorial effects with doxorubicin (DOX) were evaluated in vitro and in vivo. RESULTS: RK3 potently suppressed OS growth and metastasis in vitro and in vivo without significant systemic toxicity. Mechanistically, molecular docking predicted that RK3 binds to PRMT5, and RK3 treatment downregulated PRMT5 expression, which was associated with enhanced FBW7-GPX4 interaction, increased GPX4 ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, thereby promoting iron-dependent lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis. In combination with doxorubicin, RK3 markedly enhanced chemosensitivity and tumor suppression compared to monotherapy. CONCLUSION: Ginsenoside RK3 inhibits OS potentially through the PRMT5/GPX4 axis to promote ferroptosis and enhances the sensitivity of tumors to doxorubicin, demonstrating a favorable safety profile. These findings suggest the PRMT5/GPX4 axis as a potential therapeutic target and position RK3 as a promising candidate for chemoresistant OS.

articles.title: Cotinus coggygria Scop. extract-loaded polycaprolactone/hyaluronic acid nanofibers as candidate wound dressings: in vitro characterization, cytocompatibility and antibacterial evaluation.
articles.abstract: Cotinus coggygria Scop. (Anacardiaceae) possesses antibacterial, antioxidant, anticancer, and wound-healing properties. Hyaluronic acid (HA), a key extracellular matrix component, supports tissue regeneration. In this study, electrospun polycaprolactone (PCL) nanofibers containing C. coggygria extract and HA were developed as wound dressings. Optimized polymer solutions and electrospinning parameters were used according to material composition. Nanofibers were characterized by contact angle measurements, texture analysis, scanning electron microscopy, and in vitro cell culture assays. The fiber diameters ranged from 300 to 700 nm, and contact angle decreased to 65.3°, indicating improved hydrophilicity due to HA and C. coggygria extract incorporation. The addition of extract and HA yielded a maximum tensile strength of 2.40 MPa. After 24 h of exposure, the F5 maintained L929 fibroblast viability above 80% across the entire tested range (0.062-1 mg/mL). At 48 h, F5 produced the lowest apoptotic (6% ± 1%) and necrotic (10% ± 1%) indices among the extract-containing fibers at 1 mg/mL, indicating cytocompatibility towards L929 fibroblasts under the conditions tested. Antibacterial tests revealed inhibition zones of 21 ± 0 mm against Staphylococcus aureus and 6 ± 1 mm against Escherichia coli. Overall, PCL nanofibers incorporating C. coggygria extract and HA demonstrate promising potential for wound healing applications owing to their favorable mechanical properties, high biocompatibility, and notable antibacterial activity.

articles.title: CD38 inhibition increases neuronal survival and reduces α-synuclein in vitro, elevates brain NAD+, and reduces motor deficits in a Parkinson's disease model.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), an essential cofactor for multiple cellular processes, is critical for cellular health. NAD+ declines with age due to reduced biosynthesis and increased consumption. This causes cellular dysfunction, which exacerbates and contributes to the pathology of age-related CNS diseases, including Parkinson's disease (PD). CD38 is an NAD+-consuming enzyme (NADase) that increases in expression with ageing and disease, likely contributing to the age-related decline in NAD+. Genetic links between CD38 and PD provide a rationale for exploring its function in disease. METHODS: NETSseq datasets from human post-mortem brain tissue were used to assess CD38 cell-type-specific expression. The pharmacological properties of CVN14, a brain-penetrant selective inhibitor previously described by our group, were characterised using in vitro CD38 enzyme assays, selectivity profiling, pharmacokinetic and brain penetration studies, and brain NAD+ measurements in rats and mice. The effects of CD38 inhibition were evaluated in α-synuclein-challenged rat mesencephalic cultures and in a rat AAV1/2-hA53T α-synuclein model of PD. RESULTS: CD38 was highly enriched in astrocytes in the human brain. CVN14 potently inhibited recombinant human, rat, and mouse CD38, with IC50 values of 19.0, 5.1, and 2.4 nM, respectively. This compound was selective, having no activity at its closest homologue, CD157, or at other NADases. CVN14 increased brain NAD+ in rats and mice with no effect in the CD38 knockout mouse, further demonstrating its selectivity against other NADases. In a rat mesencephalic culture, CVN14 showed evidence of increasing dopaminergic neuronal survival following α-synuclein-induced toxicity and of reducing the number of neurons positive for pSer129 α-synuclein, thus supporting further investigation into a potential role for CD38 inhibition in the clearance of pathological protein. In a rat AAV1/2-hA53T α-synuclein model of PD, CVN14 improved motor function in the cylinder test. CONCLUSION: Our findings support further the investigation of CD38 inhibition as a therapeutic approach for PD. CVN14 elevated brain NAD+ in rats and mice reduced motor deficits in a rat α-synuclein model of PD and was associated with increased neuronal survival and reduced pathological α-synuclein in vitro, highlighting the therapeutic potential of CD38 inhibition in PD and other α-synucleinopathies.

articles.title: Conditioned media derived from HepG2 cells treated with phosphoeleganin synthetic-derived compound PE/2 improve cytokine balance and metabolic response in 3T3-L1 adipocytes.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The liver-adipose axis regulates insulin sensitivity and lipid metabolism, and its dysregulation contributes to metabolic disorders. PE/2, a semisynthetic derivative of the marine natural product phosphoeleganin, reduces IL-6 expression and secretion, enhancing insulin sensitivity in liver cells (HepG2). However, its role in liver-adipose communication is unclear. METHODS: To clarify the impact of PE/2 on liver-adipose tissue crosstalk, the conditioned media approach was used. Protein and mRNA levels were analyzed by Western blot and Real-Time RT-PCR, respectively. Lipid and glucose metabolism were evaluated by Oil Red O staining and glucose consumption assays, respectively. RESULTS: Our results indicate that in 3T3-L1 adipocytes, conditioned media derived from PE/2-treated HepG2 cells (CMPE/2) increased adiponectin expression by 1.85-fold and reduced interleukin-8 and interleukin-1β mRNA levels by 43% and 52%, respectively, compared with conditioned media alone (CM). The protective adipokine phenotype induced by CMPE/2 was accompanied by 1.75-fold lipid accumulation and increased expression of adipogenic markers, including PPARγ, C/EBPα, GLUT4, and FABP4. To examine whether this profile translates into enhanced insulin sensitivity, we evaluated the insulin pathway. Interestingly, CM from insulin-stimulated HepG2 cells (CMIns) did not significantly increase insulin receptor (INSR) or Akt phosphorylation compared with CM from 3T3-L1 adipocytes. However, CM derived from HepG2 co-treated with insulin and PE/2 (CMIns+PE/2) increased INSR and Akt phosphorylation by 2.13- and 1.63-fold, respectively, compared to CM, and by 1.83- and 1.42-fold, respectively, compared to CMIns. Consistently, 3T3-L1 glucose consumption significantly improved in the presence of CMIns+PE/2. Treatment with the PI3K/Akt inhibitor LY294002 reversed the effects of CMIns+PE/2. Finally, supplementing recombinant IL-6 into CMPE/2-treated cells reduced the effect of this compound on the expression of inflammatory and adipogenic genes and on glucose consumption in 3T3-L1 adipocytes, corroborating the hypothesis that IL-6 is involved in the action mediated by PE/2. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that PE/2 improves the metabolic-inflammatory profile in adipocytes by modulating hepatocyte-adipocyte crosstalk, highlighting its implication for metabolic dysfunctions associated with impaired liver-adipose communication.

articles.title: Engineered hyalurosomal gel co-delivering citicoline sodium and nifedipine for potential glaucoma management: formulation and pharmacodynamic evaluation.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Glaucoma is a neurodegenerative ocular disorder that requires multi-targeted therapeutic strategies to counteract intraocular pressure (IOP) elevation and oxidative stress-mediated retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) loss. This study developed an innovative hyalurosomal hydrogel platform co-delivering Nifedipine (NFD, a calcium channel blocker that promotes ocular vasodilation and IOP reduction) and Citicoline sodium (CTC, a potent neuroprotective and antioxidant agent) as a potential topical therapeutic approach for glaucoma. METHODS: NFD-loaded hyalurosomes (NFD-HAs) were prepared using thin-film hydration and statistically optimized via a D-Optimal design. The optimized formulation (NFD-OF) was probe-sonicated, combined with CTC, and incorporated into an HPMC hydrogel. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION: Sonicated NFD-OF displayed nanosized spherical vesicles (198.6 ± 23.1 nm), high entrapment efficiency (70.7 ± 1.8%), and stable zeta potential (-39.1 ± 1.3 mV). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis confirmed the distinct spherical morphology, non-aggregated state, and structural integrity of NFD-OF. The final CTC/NFD-OF gel exhibited pseudoplastic shear-thinning flow, an optimal ocular pH (6.9 ± 0.02), and sustained release over 24 h (65.5% for NFD and 99.5% for CTC). The dual gel demonstrated superior free radical scavenging capability (IC50 = 16.44±0.7 μg/mL) compared to free NFD (219.43 μg/mL) and CTC (234.62 μg/mL). Confocal microscopy confirmed a 2.2-fold enhancement in transcorneal penetration depth (110 μm) compared with the control solution (50 μm). In vivo pharmacodynamic evaluation revealed a significantly higher maximum IOP decrease (51.85 ± 8.2%), extended mean residence time (8.9 ± 2.7 h), and increased relative exposure (AUC0-∞ = 494.1 ± 191.9) compared to commercial Xola™ eye drops (36.4 ± 5.9% max IOP decrease, AUC0-∞ = 182.8 ± 33.7). Terminal gamma sterilization preserved physicochemical characteristics and release profiles. Draize and histopathological assays confirmed excellent ocular tolerability. Overall, the CTC/NFD-OF gel demonstrated promising ocular hypotensive activity and safety, supporting its potential as a multifunctional topical therapeutic approach for glaucoma.

articles.title: Cost-effectiveness analysis of cetuximab for the treatment of head and neck cancers in India.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Head and neck cancers (HNC) comprise 5% of all malignancies worldwide. Cetuximab is the first targeted therapy to demonstrate a significant survival benefit in patients with locally advanced HNC (LAHNC) and recurrent or metastatic HNC (R/MHNC). In view of this, we undertook this economic evaluation to ascertain the costs and health benefits associated with (i) the use of RT + CTX over RT alone for LAHNC patients who are ineligible for cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy and (ii) CT + CTX over CT alone for R/MHNC patients from the perspective of Indian healthcare system. METHODS: A Markov model was constructed to assess the lifetime costs and health outcomes using cetuximab in combination with radiotherapy (RT + CTX) for treatment of cisplatin-ineligible LAHNC (Analysis I), and cetuximab in combination with platinum-based chemotherapy (CT + CTX) for treatment of R/MHNC patients in India (Analysis II). Using an abridged societal perspective lifetime costs and quality adjusted life years (QALYs) were evaluated, discounting future costs and consequences at 3% annually. For both the analyses, costs of original as well as biosimilar cetuximab were evaluated. The cost-effectiveness was assessed in terms of incremental cost effectiveness ratio (ICER) which was compared against a threshold of 1-time per capita gross domestic product (GDP) for India in 2024-25 (₹ 247,045; US$ 2,697). RESULTS: Adding biosimilar cetuximab to radiotherapy for cisplatin-ineligible LAHNC patients resulted in 2.73 (95% CI: 2.11-3.30) QALYs, while adding biosimilar cetuximab to platinum-based chemotherapy for R/MHNC resulted in 0.78 (95% CI: 0.61-0.96) QALYs over the modelled lifetime horizon. The incremental cost per QALY gained was found to be ₹ 501,320 with use of RT + CTX and ₹ 15,023,037 with use of CT + CTX. At the currently recommended willingness to pay (WTP) threshold, treatment with cetuximab is not a cost-effective treatment option for patients with LAHNC and R/MHNC patients respectively in India. A 50% reduction in the price of biosimilar would make it a cost-effective option for treatment of LAHNC in India. CONCLUSION: Strategic purchasing of biosimilar cetuximab at reduced price can provide good value for money for treatment of patients with LAHNC.

articles.title: Metabolite profiling and in vitro biological activities of an endophytic Cladosporium sp. AUMC 15471 isolated from Origanum syriacum L.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Endophytic fungi associated with the za'atar plant (O. syriacum L.) remain largely underexplored despite their potential as sources of bioactive natural products. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to characterize the endophytic fungus Cladosporium sp. AUMC 15471 recovered from Origanum syriacum leaves and to investigate its chemical profile and biological activities. METHODS: Identification of Cladosporium sp. was achieved by morphological and molecular approaches. Comprehensive metabolite profiling of the ethyl acetate (EtOAc) crude extract was conducted using complementary chromatographic and mass spectrometric techniques, including gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS), high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). RESULTS: GC-MS analysis tentatively annotated 32 volatile and semi-volatile compounds based on mass spectral database matching and retention index comparison, predominantly monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes, and fatty alcohols. Targeted LC-MS/MS analysis detected 11 metabolites that were assigned based on retention time and mass-spectrometric characteristics in comparison with authentic reference standards. Several of these metabolites have not previously been reported in an endophytic Cladosporium sp. associated with O. syriacum. The EtOAc crude extract exhibited moderate antioxidant activity in the DPPH assay (IC50 = 230.21 ± 5.96 μg/mL). It also showed low cytotoxic activity against HepG2 hepatocellular carcinoma cells (IC50 = 93.43 μg/mL), with cell death involving both apoptotic and necrotic pathways. In addition, the extract displayed antibacterial activity against six bacterial species comprising five foodborne bacterial pathogens and one an opportunistic equine pathogen, with inhibition rates of 67.37% ± 2.45% against Staphylococcus aureus and 59.39% ± 1.24% against Campylobacter jejuni. CONCLUSION: Collectively, these findings indicate that Cladosporium sp. associated with O. syriacum is a promising source of chemically diverse metabolites with potential biological activities.

articles.title: Baseline mucosal transcriptomic endotypes stratify healing capacity and biologic therapy outcomes in ulcerative colitis: an integrative multi-cohort study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Numerous baseline mucosal transcriptomic signatures have been proposed to stratify therapeutic outcomes in ulcerative colitis (UC), but cross-cohort transferability is frequently undermined by platform heterogeneity, endpoint/timepoint differences, and drug-specific biases. The resulting lack of a biologic-agnostic molecular baseline has limited clinical translation and prospective trial design. METHODS: We integratively re-analyzed endpoint-linked baseline mucosal transcriptomes from seven public UC GEO series (778 unique baseline samples), with three additional public accessions used for disease-activity and contextual analyses. The primary response/healing synthesis used five study slices spanning anti-TNF, anti-integrin, and etrolizumab-treated cohorts. Unsupervised decomposition identified baseline endotypes, and endotype-outcome associations were estimated within each cohort (OR per 1-SD increase) and summarized by random-effects cross-cohort pooling with heterogeneity reporting, rank/seed sensitivity analyses, endpoint-restricted summaries, and negative controls. RESULTS: Across five primary response/healing study slices, an epithelial barrier endotype (EPITHELIAL_BARRIER/NMF_C3) was associated with higher odds of response/healing (random-effects cross-cohort pooling OR = 3.171, 95% CI 1.491-6.744), whereas macrophage-inflammation and lymphoid/complement-stromal axes (MACROPHAGE_INFLAMMATION/NMF_C1 and LYMPHOID_COMPLEMENT_STROMAL/NMF_C2) were associated with lower odds of response/healing (OR = 0.359, 0.175-0.735; OR = 0.378, 0.220-0.651). The epithelial estimate was largest in GSE73661 but remained significant in the five-study leave-one-out summary after excluding that cohort (OR = 2.547, 95% CI 1.271-5.105). Cross-mechanism evaluation included UNIFI ustekinumab week-8 mucosal healing (UST arm n = 358; EPITHELIAL_BARRIER OR = 4.483, 2.263-8.881) and directionally consistent effects in etrolizumab. Endotype axes were supported by independent single-cell localization (FDR = 0.0026). Treatment-interaction tests were imprecise and did not establish drug-class-specific prediction. In cohort-heldout prediction, AUC ranged from 0.717 to 0.758, but calibration was variable. A network-based therapeutic prioritization was enriched for UC-approved agents (AUC = 0.741; permutation p = 6.0 × 10- 4) and is presented as hypothesis-generating. CONCLUSION: Baseline mucosal endotypes stratify healing capacity and therapeutic outcomes across public cohorts, with orthogonal support from single-cell localization. These findings support prospective evaluation as biologic-agnostic outcome stratifiers rather than established drug-specific predictive biomarkers.

articles.title: Rocavorexant, a novel, selective orexin-1 receptor antagonist: Safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics in healthy adults and individuals with opioid use disorder.
articles.abstract: AIMS: Rocavorexant (INDV-2000), a selective orexin-1 receptor antagonist, reduces drug self-administration and anxiety in nonclinical studies. This Phase 1 programme evaluated the safety, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of rocavorexant in healthy volunteers and treatment-seeking individuals with opioid use disorder (OUD). METHODS: Two double-blinded Phase I studies were conducted: a first-in-human, single-ascending dose (SAD) study administering 1 to 720 mg under fasting condition with a food-effect arm (360 mg, fasting vs. fed); and a multiple-ascending dose (MAD) study evaluating up to 400 mg twice daily for up to 28 days in healthy volunteers, followed by an open-label cohort enrolling individuals with OUD who received 400 mg twice daily during co-administration with buprenorphine/naloxone and after discontinuation. RESULTS: Rocavorexant was rapidly absorbed with a mean plasma terminal half-life of 2-5 h. Plasma exposure after single doses increased dose proportionally for the area under the curve (AUC0-inf) and less than dose proportionally for maximum plasma concentration (Cmax). A high-fat meal increased rocavorexant Cmax by 62% (90% confidence interval [CI] of geometric mean ratio [GMR] 1.47-1.79) without affecting AUC0-inf (GMR 0.90; 90% CI: 0.74-1.10). Steady-state was achieved by Day 2 with minimal accumulation. Buprenorphine/naloxone co-administration increased rocavorexant AUC by 21% (GMR 90% CI: 1.01-1.45), with minor change in Cmax (GMR 1.10; 90% CI: 0.94-1.28). Rocavorexant was safe and well tolerated; somnolence was the most frequent adverse event. In the OUD cohort, rocavorexant helped manage opioid withdrawal following buprenorphine/naloxone discontinuation. CONCLUSION: Rocavorexant demonstrated favourable safety, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic characteristics supporting further clinical evaluation for OUD.

articles.title: Multi-omics indicating the risk of organochlorines to liver cancer.
articles.abstract: The incidence and mortality rates of liver cancer remain consistently high worldwide, with China having the highest rates globally. The causes of liver cancer are multifactorial. This study focuses on identifying specific targets that continuously contribute to cellular damage after exposure to environmental organic chlorine compounds (OCCs), ultimately increasing the risk of liver cancer development. Liver cancer-related data were obtained from the GEO and TCGA databases. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were analyzed using the "limma" package in R. WGCNA was employed to identify co-expression modules of highly correlated genes in liver cancer. Targets for six representative OCCs-trichloromethane, carbon tetrachloride, PCB28, PCB52, TCDD, and DDT-were retrieved from the PharmGKB, STITCH 4.0, CTD, PharmMapper, and SuperPred databases. Liver cancer-related targets were extracted from the TTD, GeneCards, Digsee, DisGeNET, OMIM, and CTD databases. A "OCCs-key targets-liver cancer" network was constructed using Cytoscape 3.8.1. Core targets were selected through cancer risk prognostic models to further investigate their roles in cancer initiation and progression. GO, KEGG, and disease enrichment analyses were performed using the core targets. The correlation between core targets and 22 types of infiltrating immune cells was analyzed. Molecular docking and dynamics simulations were conducted to verify the binding affinities between OCCs and these core proteins. A total of 195 common targets between OCCs and liver cancer were identified. After performing PPI analysis, 85 key targets were selected to construct a "OCCs-key targets-liver cancer" network. TTK, KPNA2, CDKN3, EZH2, and CPEB3 were identified as core targets through the cancer risk prognostic model. GO enrichment analysis revealed that the core targets were primarily involved in the regulation of the mitotic cell cycle. KEGG enrichment analysis confirmed a strong association between these targets and chemical carcinogenesis, as well as cell cycle regulation. Disease enrichment analysis indicated that the core targets were significantly linked to neoplasms, particularly liver cancer. Immunoinfiltration analysis suggested that tumors may promote immune evasion by increasing the expression of immunosuppressive cells while decreasing the levels of activated immune cells. Molecular docking and dynamics simulations identified key binding interactions, amino acid residues, and binding energies, further confirming strong binding affinities between OCCs and the core targets. This study integrates network toxicology, machine learning, WGCNA, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and immunoinfiltration analysis, providing evidence that prolonged exposure to OCCs may increase the risk of liver cancer development.

articles.title: Immune-related adverse reactions across multiple systems in a non-small cell lung cancer patient induced by immune checkpoint inhibitors: a case report and literature review.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have revolutionized the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), while overlapping multi-system immune-related adverse events (irAEs) are life-threatening and pose great clinical challenges. CASE DESCRIPTION: A 74-year-old male patient with stage IIIA lung squamous cell carcinoma developed bilateral ptosis, blurred vision, abnormal thyroid function, elevated muscle enzymes and cardiac biomarkers after two cycles of toripalimab combined with chemotherapy. He was diagnosed with ICI-induced myositis, myocarditis and thyroiditis. ICIs were discontinued immediately. Glucocorticoids, methimazole and levothyroxine were administered sequentially according to disease progression. The patient recovered well and underwent lobectomy successfully. CONCLUSION: Elderly individuals complicated with pre-existing cardiovascular diseases are susceptible to severe immune-related adverse events. Early identification of overlapping multi-system irAEs, timely drug withdrawal and standardized immunosuppressive therapy are essential. Endocrine-immune-related adverse reactions exhibit dynamic evolution; for instance, thyroid toxicity may progress from a hyperthyroid phase to hypothyroidism, necessitating individualized monitoring and replacement therapy according to different stages of thyroid function.
